A comprehensive study on the counterterm method for analyzing charged, rotating black brane solutions is presented, taking into account the influence of angular momentum and mass. This approach is applied to the Einstein-Maxwell theory and its extensions, including corrections due to gravitational perturbation theory. The focus is on the impact of these corrections on the counterterm method, as well as the resulting solutions, to ensure accurate holographic calculations for systems built from them. Deep neural networks have demonstrated exceptional performance on various low-resolution image classification tasks but are difficult to transfer between different domains. Unlike existing studies that focus on input data adaptations, we investigate how graph neural networks (GNNs) learn and transfer knowledge across tasks. Our findings reveal that GNNs exhibit lower transferability compared to other deep networks, and we demonstrate that this is largely due to their tendency to identify persistent community structures in the data rather than specific visual characteristics. Consequently, we observe that GNNs often fail to generalize between tasks with distinct community structures in addition to visual content. However, we identify the community similarity between tasks as a crucial factor influencing GNN transferability and develop a training approach that adjusts GNNs to focus on robust, stable community features. Our method achieves improved transfer learning performance on real-world and synthetic datasets. The associated code can be found on our GitHub repository at https://github.com/mattmortimer/graph-neural-networks. Our research contributes to an understanding of GNNs as well as other deep networks by highlighting their limitations in transfer learning. Furthermore, our work provides insight into the learned representations as well as how graph-based inductive bias affects deep network behavior. Our research also indicates that graph-based transfer learning remains an underdeveloped area of study. Our findings suggest that input adaptation methods may not always be necessary or effective, and instead, graph-based transfer learning strategies could be more directly beneficial. Our research suggests that graph-based transfer learning strategies may be more effective and necessary for GNNs in particular. Our research could lead to the development of novel transfer learning adaptations and strategies specifically for graph neural networks, ultimately enabling the creation of more robust and transferable GNNs capable of generalizing to new domains with minimal data. Our research may also inspire the design of new graph-based adaptation methods to complement existing deep network transfer learning methods. Our research could also be extended to other deep network architectures to explore how graph-based transfer learning can be used to improve the transferability of models beyond GNNs. Our research may also provide insights into the design of new graph-based adaptation methods to support the transfer of graph data structures, potentially leading to the transfer of GNNs trained on abstract graph representations to other domains. Our research could also be applied to the transfer of GNNs trained on image data to other modalities such as text or depth, ultimately enabling the transfer of knowledge between different domains with minimal data. A novel latent variable model is introduced, based on the Indian Buffet Process, to address data sparsity and cold start issues in recommender systems. The model diverges from conventional user-item rating matrices by instead creating a set of user, item, and shared features. The IBP-based inference enables user, item, and feature memberships without the need for an extensive number of features, thus addressing data sparsity effectively. The model also overcomes the cold start problem by allowing new items and features to be incorporated, thus enhancing performance in large-scale recommender systems. Evaluations using public datasets demonstrate the model's superiority over existing models, while highlighting potential trade-offs in feature usage. The empirical findings suggest several strategies to balance recall and precision, involving the optimization of parameters that influence feature usage. The source code is available at https://github.com/ucf-data/ibp-recommendation for reproduction of the experiments. The model's performance can be leveraged to recommend not only items, but also features, thus providing a novel direction for future research. The proposed approach may also benefit other applications, such as multi-label classification and clustering, by providing an explicit representation of features. The theoretical underpinnings of the model are explored in the appendix through an analysis of its marginal likelihood and posterior concentration parameters. The model's runtime efficiency is demonstrated by its performance on a Yelp dataset with 1 million ratings, taking approximately 1 second to run. We suggest a novel approach to superconducting quantum circuits that can be used to create complex quantum devices tailored to the needs of current quantum technology advancements. Our proposal specifically addresses the development of devices involving a single atom. With the integration of superconducting circuits, researchers have made notable progress in coherently controlling multiple quantum systems in recent years. The achievement of reaching the quantum computing era depends on overcoming several challenges associated with multi-frequency coherent control, atom-cavity system coordination, and efficient single-photon emission. To address these challenges, we introduce a central wire in our structure, which serves to coordinate quantum components during operation, enhance single-photon emission, and reduce unwanted interference effects. Our device consists of a Qubit-LS (low- and high-frequency) system, a central wire, and a highly transmissive photon cavity, all connected in a row. When an electromagnetic signal is applied to the central wire, it couples with the cavity, producing a highly transmissible evanescent wave, which coordinates the Qubit-LS and cavity frequencies, making it possible to achieve entanglement between the two. Meanwhile, a highly transmissive photon cavity facilitates efficient single-photon emission from the Qubit-LS. Our device has been shown to improve the efficiency of single-photon emission by enhancing the coherence of the Qubit-LS. With the implementation of appropriate control sequences, our device can achieve multi-frequency coherent control, demonstrating its potential in the development of complex quantum devices. Furthermore, our device has been used to model the single-photon double-slit experiment, demonstrating that it can efficiently coordinate the measurement of Qubit-LS and simulate the interference of photons in the cavity. Our device offers a unique platform for the simulation and realization of quantum computing concepts and provides an innovative solution to the challenges of current quantum technology advancements. The design of our device has been verified using an open-source software package available at http://gitub.com/ChengliangWu/SLDRCShare. Furthermore, our device has been shown to improve the efficiency of single-photon emission by enhancing the coherence of the Qubit-LS, which has potential applications in the field of single-atom quantum optics. Our device design offers an innovative approach to the realization of single-atom quantum optics, which has significant potential in the development of future quantum technologies. Our study provides an essential reference point for future research and can inspire innovative device designs tailored to the needs of current quantum technology advancements. Ultimately, our device has the potential to revolutionize the field of quantum technology

Given a function $p$, which specifies the exponent for the integrand, and a function $b$, which defines the phase and amplitude of the integrand, we derive an estimator for the oscillatory integral. The conditions for the phase and amplitude functions are relatively standard but require the phase function to be concave. However, the amplitude function must satisfy specific regularity requirements, with its derivatives being bounded and converging at a comparable rate to the sampling measure. We employ a novel approach, which combines an adaptive truncation technique and a weighted Lévy-Hahn decomposition, to achieve this goal. As a result, we establish a strong and weak law of large numbers for the oscillatory integral, with corresponding rates of convergence. This research also explores the asymptotic behavior of oscillatory integrals, demonstrating both strong and weak convergence, and derives an error bound for the difference between the estimator and the oscillatory integral. The Synthetic Control Method, widely used in policy evaluation, relies on the availability of relevant time-series data from the treated unit and comparable control units.  Typically, researchers must discard noisy control observations, which are often unable to participate in estimation due to missing or disqualifying data.  We propose a new method to leverage these previously unusable control observations by utilizing their time-series information from other treated units.  We achieve this by adapting control observation time-series with those from the treated unit using unsupervised machine learning techniques.  We then calculate the adapted control observation's similarity to the treated unit using the distance between their time-series differences.  With this adapted control observation similarity calculated, we can estimate Synthetic Control weights using a weighted average of the treated unit and multiple adapted control observations.  We show that our estimator has asymptotic efficiency comparable to the best possible estimator and simulate results indicating superior performance on real-world datasets and theoretical benchmarks.  We apply our novel estimator to estimate the impact of Russia's 2006 auto-insurance policy dataset.  Our study was supported by the National Science Foundation grant CNS-1646380. In graph machine learning, numerous widely-used methods are compromised by sensitive information in node attributes, as demonstrated by recent studies. To address this issue, local differential privacy is employed to safeguard against inferred node data. Local differential privacy has shown promise in other areas, such as private deep learning. However, its application in graph machine learning is particularly challenging due to the intricate connections between nodes. Previous work using local differential privacy in graph machine learning has been limited, with most methods neglecting node attribute protection or relying on simplified methods that don't form a comprehensive mathematical framework. In this research, we provide a comprehensive framework for local differential privacy in graph machine learning and its associated mathematical foundations. Additionally, we develop and evaluate more sophisticated methods that incorporate local differential privacy and demonstrate improved performance compared to previous methods and baselines. Our results are based on an extended version of the Semi-Synthetic Node Attribute Protection (SNAP) dataset. This research is made available on a GitHub repository. 

Note: This research is an expansion of our previous work in ArXiv [2021], with significant extensions to the methodology, including the development of a more sophisticated method, a more comprehensive framework, and a formal mathematical foundation for local differential privacy in graph machine learning. Further details can be found in our technical report [ArXiv:2109.10375, 2021].

A novel local search algorithm, dubbed E2LS, has been designed to efficiently solve two key combinatorial optimization problems: the Subgraph-Encoded Union-Slack Flow (SUKP) and the Binary Mixed-Combinatorial Packing Problem (BMCP). E2LS employs a two-stage local search strategy that initially utilizes an exact solver to identify high-quality initial solutions, which are then refined using tailored local operations to optimize the solution set. To achieve this, E2LS leverages a hybrid configuration of elementary and composite moves rooted in graph theory, as well as a balance-based reconfiguration method. By incorporating the exact solver at the initial stage, E2LS demonstrates enhanced solution quality compared to other local search methods. Moreover, the algorithm's efficiency is further amplified by introducing a balance-based reconfiguration method during the second stage. Computational results indicate that E2LS exhibits a high solution quality and computational speed in solving SUKP and BMCP. Additionally, the algorithm's superiority is confirmed by its ability to produce high-quality integer solutions for the Maximum Subgraph-Encoded Flow (MSF) problem when combined with a parameterized binary optimization approach. Notably, E2LS outperforms other local search algorithms in solving the SUKP and BMCP, while its performance on the MSF problem surpasses that of a commercial solver, which fails to match its performance on similar large-scale instances. On the Binary Metric TSP, E2LS's performance is comparable to state-of-the-art results achieved by other methods. Further analysis of the algorithm's performance demonstrates that for a given time limit, E2LS produces more balanced integer solutions than the exact solver. Consequently, the proposed E2LS algorithm is established as a versatile local search algorithm, effective across various flow and packing problems, including graph theory and combinatorial optimization. Its high solution quality, computational speed, and adaptability make it an ideal choice for solving SUKP, BMCP, and related problem variants. By employing a local search strategy, E2LS can be easily integrated with other methods, such as parameterized binary optimization, to produce high-quality integer solutions for the MSF problem. Churn prevention has emerged as a critical concern for the customer retention department in top companies, necessitating the development of accurate models that can forecast customer departure. The key challenge lies in determining the length of time-series data needed for successful prediction. In this paper, we investigate the influence of time-series history using classical statistical and machine learning methods. Our analysis reveals that the model's performance improves with longer time-series history, but only up to a point, demonstrating the concept of diminishing returns. Specifically, we find that models trained on 3 to 6 time-steps exhibit optimal prediction accuracy, illustrating the law of diminishing margins in machine learning. Our findings also reveal that models based on recurrent neural networks are more resilient to overfitting than their classical counterparts, requiring longer history to degrade performance. Furthermore, we present an adaptive approach to selecting time-series history, utilizing a Bayesian model selection metric to dynamically choose the length. Our results show that this adaptive method matches or surpasses the performance of models trained with optimally determined history lengths. In practical terms, our work suggests that using 5 to 10 months of historical data yields the best outcome for customer churn prediction. In robotic path planning, ensuring that trajectories are robust to system uncertainties is crucial to avoid unexpected failures. Current methods typically minimize the chance of failure by maintaining a safety margin, but do not account for potential model inaccuracies, leading to an excessive conservative approach. In this paper, we present an innovative solution to address this issue by incorporating multiple uncertain system perspectives to create a more accurate model and thus a more aggressive trajectory with the same level of reliability as existing approaches. The proposed method transforms the path planning problem from a binary success or failure issue to a continuous performance optimization, measured by a hyper-elastic distance metric that accounts for model errors. A novel numerical solution to this problem is developed using an advanced per-point optimization method, resulting in a more efficient and less conservative approach than existing techniques, demonstrated through experiments on a hexapod robot. The results show our approach outperforms existing methods by a factor of 2 in trajectory length while maintaining the same level of failure prevention during real-world field tests. We investigate the behavior of nonlocal solutions to conservation laws with convolution kernels as their discrete counterpart, particularly in relation to weak limits. By examining the properties of the convolution kernel, we demonstrate that all nonlocal solutions converge to an entropy-admissible solution, building on the work of Carrillo and Vietor in \cite{CV17}. Moreover, we expand on their research in three specific areas: (i) allowing for a wide range of integrability conditions, (ii) considering general discrete systems rather than just discrete velocity structures, and (iii) examining the rate of convergence in the discrete setting. In a discrete context, we show that the outcomes rely on the kernel's characteristics at its edges, leading to a faster convergence when these are well-defined. Conversely, when they are ambiguous, a greater discrete density is required for the results to hold. Our work in this area not only provides insights into the behavior of discrete conservation laws, but also contributes to the understanding of general measure-valued solutions to continuous conservation laws. Gaussian processes are excellent choices for modeling systems where observations are noisy and multidimensional, yet there are few practical methods for sampling their posterior distributions. The recent development of pathwise conditioning has improved the efficiency of sampling Gaussian process posters, though primarily in cases with relatively small numbers of data inputs. To address this limitation, we've created an algorithm combining pathwise conditioning with kernel flow that is capable of handling larger numbers of data inputs. The algorithm replaces the standard white noise inputs in kernel flow with conditioned Gaussian variables, which can be approximated using a tree structure for faster computation. We've demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach by training it on large datasets, such as images. The resulting model allows for the drawing of multiple samples from the Gaussian process posterior, which can then be used to make predictions and an uncertainty budget can be tracked. The uncertainty budget can be utilized to determine when it is necessary to augment the dataset with additional data for improved predictive accuracy. Pathwise kernel flow significantly enhances the efficiency of sampling Gaussian process posters and facilitates the development of more accurate and uncertain models based on these processes. To refine this estimation, we established a relationship between the UAV's position and the signal power it receives, represented as a function of the UAV's altitude and horizontal distance from the sensors. In addition, we created a probabilistic model based on various assumptions to generate random positions for the UAV and the ground sensors. Our results indicate that the estimated signal power and measured signal power exhibit a strong linear correlation. The Large Underground Neutrino Detector (DUNE) is a powerful experiment designed to study the properties of subatomic particles, particularly long-distance interactions like proton decay. DUNE's deep underground location and massive liquid argon detector, capable of detecting small amounts of energy, make it an ideal setup to study this phenomenon. Furthermore, DUNE's design features a large number of target protons, allowing it to detect rare signals, specifically the decay of protons into wimps, while also studying more common neutrino interactions and informing the development of new theories to explain the behavior of subatomic particles. The current study examines the potential of DUNE to identify the decay of protons into wimps by analyzing data from 1982 to 1985 with a 32-kiloton near detector and 42-kiloton far detector, and demonstrates that it can identify signals consistent with previously established limits on this phenomenon by the IMB and Frejus collaborations. The study also shows that DUNE can establish a more than 15-fold improvement in its ability to identify these signals, and that this phenomenon can potentially be studied at scales of hundreds of kilometers with liquid argon detectors, and at scales of thousands of kilometers with water-based detectors. Accurately interpreting the outcomes of machine learning models is crucial, and a particular challenge arises when dealing with complex datasets. This paper introduces an advanced method of feature importance assessment based on the SHAP framework, which enables global and local explanations by assigning meaningful values to each embedded document in our model. By leveraging these values, we are able to evaluate the performance of our model in relation to established information retrieval metrics. Furthermore, our method facilitates the creation of a feature importance map and enables the identification of crucial terms within relevant documents, allowing for a deeper understanding of our model's decision-making processes. Our approach is presented in the context of a comparative analysis of BERT models for natural language inference and natural language document ranking. Experimental results demonstrate that our model achieves state-of-the-art performance while providing valuable insights into the importance of embedded document words. This research aims to inspire the development of more effective machine learning models and inform information retrieval systems, while showcasing the SHAP framework as a powerful tool for feature importance assessment and facilitating the interpretation of our embedded documents. Overall, our method offers an innovative approach to feature importance assessment and facilitates the interpretation of our machine learning models in the context of information retrieval applications. With continuous advancements in large language models, such as those discussed in Section 7, our model is well-positioned to benefit from these developments. Ultimately, our research demonstrates the SHAP framework to be a versatile tool for feature importance assessment in machine learning models. Further research is needed to bridge the gap between feature importance assessment and human-level explanation; an area that warrants exploration in the context of information retrieval systems and machine learning models. This paper introduces a high-level programming language called VOPL for describing virtual reality objects called VOs, which are defined by their 3D shape and behavior. VOPL enables VR developers to focus on the system's overall structure by breaking down a VR application into separate components of VOs and viewing the variations in these components as different instantiations of a template, considering multiple instantiations as different interpretations of a single concept. VOPL allows developers to define a VO's behavior using a set of rules, which are written in a probabilistic logic programming language called ProbLog. A key aspect of VOPL is its ability to decouple a VR application's logic from its visual presentation, enabling developers to create VOs that can be recognized and rendered by other VR objects, which can be designed or created by other developers, promoting modularity and reusability in VR design. The paper presents a case study on a VR simulation of human flight to demonstrate the language's capabilities and discusses potential applications of VOPL in designing human-VR-agent interactions. Reinforcement learning via policy gradient descent faces a major challenge in estimating gradients due to its high variance. This work introduces a new variances reduction approach called variance reduction based experience replay (VRER) that enables multiple views of the data to reduce variance. Our research reveals that VRER can be combined with several variance reduction techniques such as James-Stein and maximum likelihood estimation. We implement a novel experience replay framework, ER-PG, by integrating VRER with a James-Stein estimator, which offers two settings: ER-JS, which reuses experiences under non-convex objectives and ER-JS*, which projects them under convex objectives. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that ER-PG achieves a lower bound for the gradient variance. Our experimental results on various benchmark problems show that ER-PG significantly reduces the required number of samples in comparison to existing methods. Our work also reveals that experience replay can be viewed as a specific instance of state representation learning. Furthermore, our research reveals that our integrated framework, ER-PG, is a particular instance of a more general approach called state representation learning. Our experimental results validate our theoretical findings. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/duhng/ER-PRX. We employ path-integral representation via the Cho-Della Torre transformation to convert the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and superbosonization formula into each other, proving their equivalence through an explicit, detailed derivation. To verify the transformation's validity, we use Fourier transformation and elementary integration to analyze both two- and three-dimensional cases. Additionally, we apply path-integral representation to derive an alternative form of the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation, thereby providing a new approach to superbosonization formula and reverse transformation. Furthermore, we apply our method to solve the $O(2)$ nonlinear $\sigma$-model at zero temperature, first performing superbosonization on the Lagrangian to yield an effective action, then use Fourier transformation to convert the effective action into momentum space and derive a new, explicit form. We then use the new effective action to perform Fourier transformation and compute the Monte-Carlo integral, ultimately obtaining the effective action in momentum space. To verify our results, we compute the momentum-space effective action for the $O(3)$ nonlinear $\sigma$-model at zero temperature, first performing superbosonization on the Lagrangian to yield an effective action, then use Fourier transformation to convert the effective action into momentum space and derive a new, explicit form. We then use the new effective action to perform Fourier transformation and compute the Monte-Carlo integral, ultimately obtaining the effective action in momentum space. By comparing our results with existing literature, we verify the accuracy of our method. Finally, we apply our method to investigate the superfluidity of the $O(3)$ nonlinear $\sigma$-model with a magnetic field, first performing Fourier transformation to convert the effective action into momentum space and derive a new, explicit form, then use the new effective action to compute the Monte-Carlo integral, ultimately obtaining the effective action in momentum space. By analyzing our results, we conclude on the existence of a condensation process in the $O(3)$ nonlinear $\sigma$-model under a magnetic field. We also provide a new, explicit form of the effective action in momentum space, thereby providing a theoretical understanding of the phenomenon. Our method can be extended to various models, thereby providing a new, versatile tool for analysis. We hope our results contribute to existing literature. We examine the production of a heavy neutral lepton accompanied by a Z boson at high-energy colliders. The process involves a major contribution from lepton number violation, which stems from the mixing of a standard model electron with heavier neutral leptons. Our study focuses on the sensitivity to lepton number violation, which can be quantified through parameters $\delta_{ei}$ and $\delta_{\mu i}$. For the first time, we investigate the relevant parameter space that could be probed at the Future Circular Collider, electron collider version (ECCe), in the context of the process $e^+ e^-\to \chi^0_Z$ followed by $\chi^0 \to p \bar{p}$, using the invisible decays of a neutral lepton. Our findings suggest that the FCCe could reach sensitivities of $\delta_{ei}$ and $\delta_{\mu i}$ up to $10^{-5}$ and $10^{-7}$ respectively, given the heaviest neutral lepton mass of around 1 TeV or less. Our study further reveals that the cross-section of the process $e^0 e^-\chi^0 Z$ would be largely independent of the mixing angle $\delta_{ei}$ but heavily reliant on it when considering $\delta_{\mu i}$. Ultimately, our analysis indicates that the process $e^0 e^-\chi^0 Z$ offers a unique opportunity for constraining the relevant parameter space associated with $\delta_{\mu i}$. Our study demonstrates that the process offers an optimal sensitivity to $\delta_{\mu i}$, which can be probed up to $5\times 10^{-7}$, given certain conditions. Our findings suggest that the process offers the most favorable constraints compared to other search channels like $\mu^- \chi^0$ and $pp\chi^0$. Our study shows that the search channel $e^0 e^-\chi^0 Z$ provides the most sensitive constraints on the relevant parameter space, allowing for a discovery reach of $\delta_{\mu i}=10^{-7}$ at the FCCe. Our analysis suggests that the discovery reach could be extended to $\delta_{\mu i}=10^{-6}$ using a 1 TeV collider operating at energy $\sqrt{s}=1.5$ TeV. A new protocol, referred to as the Compact Verified Quantum Comparison (CVQC) protocol, has been created to enable the comparison and verification of large binary files using quantum computers. This CVQC protocol incorporates a compact verification mechanism that reduces the number of qubits required for comparison and verification. In our analysis, CVQC was compared to existing protocols in terms of various criteria such as communication, storage, and processing requirements. Experimental results demonstrated that CVQC outperformed these protocols in verification speed, with a significant advantage in processing time for larger files. Furthermore, CVQC exhibited a comparable level of communication and storage efficiency. This study confirms the feasibility of CVQC as a practical method for secure data transmission. In a potential future application, CVQC can be employed by cybersecurity professionals to verify their clients' data integrity by comparing transmitted data at the receiver's location and verifying it using a trusted quantum device. Additionally, CVQC can be used for secure data comparison and verification purposes, such as securely transmitting files to cloud storage services while verifying data integrity using a public quantum key less (QKL) protocol. In the future, CVQC can be used in practical applications such as secure data comparison and verification, data transmission with verification, or data transmission to quantum-enabled cloud storage services. Deep learning techniques have revolutionized image analysis with their exceptional performance, yet their limitations in diverse datasets and absence of underlying knowledge mean they may not always be the best choice. This classification reveals that such metrics can be uniquely characterized by the curvature at the singularity and a certain factor that depends on the singularity's gauge, along with either the Chern-Gauss-Bonnet form or the Kostant curvature on a certain Lie algebra. Furthermore, it has been shown that the classification of constant curvature metrics on the sphere, with a specific singularity, extends to the classification of all constant curvature metrics on the sphere, including those that have a different curvature at the singularity. In addition, it has been found that the classification of constant curvature metrics on the sphere, with a specific singularity, is connected to the classification of all harmonic forms on the sphere by showing that the obstruction to the exactness of the de Rham sequence is constant. Yet, there is still a significant gap in the simulation field, particularly in the adaptive modeling of tsunami phenomena that combine deep ocean processes with detailed accounts of coastal inundation. Furthermore, the study discusses the theoretical foundations of adaptive simulation and its future applications in efficient multi-scale simulations of complex natural phenomena. Research has long been confined to materials experiencing affine deformations, however recent studies have made significant headways in identifying non-affine behavior, particularly in the elastic range. Experimentally verifying non-affinity is complicated as it requires precise measurements of material microstructure and modeling non-affine behavior with minimal computational complexity. To address this, a new model is developed, grounded in thermodynamic principles, to describe non-affine materials and account for their distinct material parameters. Building upon this model, a new method is introduced for calculating the material's non-affine coefficient and determining if a material exhibits non-affine characteristics in the elastic range. This method involves comparing simulated material self-contact in the absence of external loads with equivalent simulations that apply a constant stretch. If the two simulations display matching energy levels and material configurations, it can be concluded that the material exhibits affine behavior, whereas significant discrepancies indicate non-affinity. To confirm non-affinity, a power-law relationship must be observed between non-affinity coefficients and load levels. Our study demonstrates the practical application of this new method using multiple case studies, which include both traditional and new materials that have never been previously analyzed. These case studies show that non-affine behavior can be observed in materials subjected to various loads, highlighting the model's versatility and accuracy. Ultimately, this work's research offers a new understanding of non-affine materials, which can expand beyond traditional polymers to include emerging materials like shape-memory alloys. On a larger scale, this work's findings can contribute to the development of new theoretical frameworks for solid mechanics that accurately capture non-affine behavior and its implications at various deformation levels. Furthermore, this work's research provides a new method to identify and distinguish between affine and non-affine regimes in materials that exploit non-affinity to achieve unexplored performance levels.

The Resilience Satisfaction Value functions, RECSV and ReSV, offer a way to quantify recoverability and durability in system specifications by providing an overall resilience assessment. However, their current formulation relies on system time-varying state information, which is often difficult to obtain in practice, due to limitations in observability. To overcome this challenge, a new approach involves developing a metric that uses only available system output data, through machine learning techniques, to estimate the RECSV and ReSV functions. This leads to the development of two output-based Resilience Satisfaction Value functions, ORECSV and OReSV, which are theoretically justified and tested using a case study on a cooling system. Analysis shows that the proposed methods are both intuitive and effective, offering a feasible solution for system resilience assessment. Furthermore, a comparison with expert evaluations reveals that the proposed methods perform well, considering they rely on limited expert knowledge and cooling system curves. Finally, a discussion highlights potential future areas for improvement, including the application of these methods to real-world systems, the incorporation of additional supervisory feedback, and the exploration of additional resilience metrics. Recent studies on planning the collision-free movements of articulated robots have shown that incorporating spatial constraints can significantly reduce the computational resources required for movement planning. However, the generation of these constraints in real-world environments is often a manual and time-consuming process. In response, we present a novel approach that leverages a 3D point cloud to automatically identify and define spatial constraints, thereby facilitating efficient movement planning in complex environments. The proposed method utilizes a novel graph structure to represent spatial constraints, enabling rapid compilation of a motion planning system capable of tackling challenging scenarios, such as warehouse robotics. In particular, we demonstrate that our constraint-based motion planner outperforms a state-of-the-art method by achieving an average of 4-fold speedup in simulation, alongside a notable 65% improvement in success rate, especially in cluttered environments where constraints are crucial. Moreover, we validate the practical applicability of our method in kinect-based autonomous warehouse settings, showcasing its potential to substantially accelerate movement planning times. The proposed method is expected to achieve even greater performance gains in scenarios where visual perception sensors continuously provide updated 3D point cloud information. The source code and source graph dataset are publicly available on our GitHub repository. Additionally, we recommend an interactive web-based visualization tool to explore our results. In this study, we investigate the uplink of a dense multiuser MIMO system, examining the sum-rate and interference issues. To address these problems, we apply group LASSO to the uplink channel precoding and receiver decoding. Group LASSO integrates elements within the same group more closely than other methods, such as conventional LASSO. As a result, group LASSO is applied to the uplink channel precoder at the transmitters and decoder at the receiver, effectively forming a collaborative framework that accounts for the transceiver pairing. Group LASSO formulates the sum-rate maximization as a convex optimization problem, which is solved efficiently using an interior-point method. To simplify the problem and reduce computational complexity, we propose a subproblem algorithm that leverages Z-axis projection, iteratively solving smaller optimization problems. Furthermore, we develop a per-stream precoder and decoder structure to minimize the number of groups, making group LASSO more practical. Numerical results demonstrate that our proposed group LASSO approach surpasses state-of-the-art methods in sum-rate performance, while also showcasing its ability to manage interference and reduce the number of groups with minimal performance degradation. Additionally, group LASSO's performance benefits from its alignment with standard optimization methods, making it more computationally efficient than other methods. Finally, we validate the effectiveness of group LASSO in identifying meaningful transceiver pairing, which is not achievable in conventional optimization methods due to their limitations in recovering sparse signals. Consider a finite harmonic map $\chi: \mathcal{T}\rightarrow \mathcal{S}$ between tropical curves $\mathcal{S}$ and $\mathcal{T}$. We define a pull-back operation on rational function semifield of $\mathcal{S}$ to that of $\mathcal{T}$ and demonstrate that it is an algebraic semifield following the pull-back of rational functions in algebraic geometry. Next, we derive a tropical version of the theorem of Ahlfors and Beurling for curves with finite harmonic maps. Furthermore, we develop a tropical version of the semistable Gauss-Manin formalism suitable for one-parameter families of curves with finite harmonic maps, and use it to prove a pull-back theorem for Betti numbers under such conditions. Ultimately, we apply our results to solve the tropical version of the classical Milnor's seminar, and investigate the pull-back of Betti numbers in relation to finite harmonic maps between tropical curves. Moreover, we extend our method to examine the pull-back of de Rham semifield and derive a tropical version of the theorem of Poincar\'e under such conditions. Finally, we apply our results to examine the pull-back of de Rham semifield and Betti numbers in the context of finite harmonic maps between tropical curves, and derive a tropical version of the classical result on pull-back of de Rham semifield and Betti numbers in algebraic geometry following the pull-back of finite maps. The addition of electric potential modifies the momentum squared in the Hamilton-Jacobi equation, leading to a diverse range of solutions. In the positive momentum region, the electric potential eliminates the first order phase transition. However, in the negative momentum region, the electric potential's effect on the momentum squared influences whether or not a black hole and anti-black hole emerge in a thin shell thick layer near the cavity's boundary. The existence of electric potential does not affect the temperature of thin shell thick layers but does alter their stability. The presence of electric potential does not change the temperature but does change the stability of thick and thin shell structures, and in certain cases, can transform a thick shell into two thin shell structures separated by a Maxima-Minima point in the momentum graph. The research indicates that the electric potential's impact on phase transitions and black hole existence in a spherical cavity is complex and multifaceted. Further exploration of these phenomena may lead to a deeper understanding of the relationship between electric potential, momentum, and thermal and electrothermal properties of thick and thin shell structures. The study also reveals that in the context of cosmological principles, the existence of electric potential does not result in any observable consequences due to its negligible effect on cosmological scales. We also introduce a new semi-supervised semi-supervisor that utilizes the labeled information from the unlabeled nodes, in contrast to traditional pseudo-labeling methods. Our experiments demonstrate that our proposed method surpasses standard pseudo-labeling in semi-supervised node classification and achieves better performance than current state-of-the-art baselines on various datasets. We find that nodal pseudo-labeling is particularly beneficial in scenarios with significant class imbalance problems. Our proposed method is flexible and can be combined with any GNN model, making it suitable for a range of datasets. This research focuses on the study of a simple wall-following robot that operates at the front of a moving vehicle, employing a distance sensor with a limited field of view. A basic mathematical model has been developed to analyze the robot's behavior by considering the sensor's field of view and its position on the vehicle. A crucial aspect of this model is its non-linear system characteristics, which give rise to a first-order partial differential equation that defines the robot's trajectory as a function of its current position and velocity. An approximate solution to this equation, suitable for scenarios where the sensor's field of view is relatively narrow, has been derived, in addition to a comprehensive analytical solution for situations where the sensor's field of view is not restricted. Both approaches have been validated through the use of a robot simulation system that is capable of modeling systems with varying fields of view and front offsets. Ultimately, our research demonstrates that a robot equipped with a distance sensor, positioned at the front of a moving vehicle, is unable to replicate the behavior of a proton-like particle flow, but can instead mimic the behavior of a negatively charged particle, with its trajectory influenced by the sensor's field of view and position, as well as the vehicle's speed and direction of movement. Consequently, for a wall-following robot to achieve its optimal performance, it is crucial to optimize its sensor placement based on its field of view and the vehicle's front offset. A design guideline for achieving this purpose has been presented in the final section of the research. Present methods for evaluating pre-processing pipelines either focus on general metrics or rely on external assessments. As a result, the effectiveness of a pre-processing pipeline can only be fully understood when its applications are tested, which is often after the pipeline has been implemented. By analyzing this method, we found that it can improve the classification layer, thus enhancing the entire pre-processing pipeline. We demonstrated this approach on two tasks, achieving an 8.6% increase in the F1 score for named entity recognition and a 4.3% increase in the F1 score for machine translation. We make the source code available at https://github.com/dvdxp/pipe-eval. Additionally, we provide a representative adaptation of this approach for the named entity recognition task using benchmark data, resulting in an F1 score of 96.59, surpassing the previously published state-of-the-art by 0.06. We report these findings in a companion paper at the 23rd ERMAR Conference. We suggest integrating this method into natural language processing frameworks, such as spaCy, to facilitate pre-processing pipeline development and optimization. In a study of Kagome materials like Ru$_c$Ge, we examined the many-body gap in chiral spin liquids as the density of plaquettes with an odd number of edges ($n_{\triangle}$) varies, finding a significant impact on the many-body gap. This is due to a fundamental "topological gap" arising from such plaquettes in a non-trivial topology, with the gap decreasing as $n_{\triangle}$ deviates from 4/9. This finding bears similarities to a recent theoretical paper on symmetry-protected topological gap closure, with the difference being a "geometric gap" closure in this case, influenced by the geometric arrangement of Kagome lattice rather than symmetry. This is in contrast to earlier theories, with our work identifying a many-body gap in chiral spin liquids for certain Kagome materials and highlighting the necessity to consider the lattice's structure in determining the gap. Furthermore, our work suggests that a non-trivial topology in these materials is not sufficient to account for their large energy scales, with the geometric arrangement of the lattice playing a crucial role instead. This is in contrast to naive expectations based on general principles for topological systems, with the actual physics observed in Ru$_c$Ge differing due to its unique combination of non-trivial topology and high energy scales. Lastly, we propose that a non-trivial geometric gap in these materials could be experimentally observed through certain methods, such as deep UV spectroscopy, capable of detecting the remaining energy degrees of freedom to very low temperatures. Deep UV spectroscopy could thus be used to directly verify the non-trivial topology of these materials by tracking how $n_{\triangle}$ changes in response to external stimuli or material adjustments, such as Ru content in Ge samples, and this method could be generally applied to other materials with a non-trivial topology. Arrays with numerous redundant antennas are crucial for sensitive astronomical observations, but their efficiency is limited by variability in antenna gains caused by atmospheric fluctuations. Real-time calibration can mitigate this issue to some extent. In our research, we analyzed how wide bands, frequency channels, and data processing influence the reliability of antenna gain stabilization in the NOEMA telescope array, utilizing data collected from various sources on the Plateau de Bure. We found that wide bands offer better stability, but may also limit survey missions that require monitoring a wide frequency range. In contrast, channels can provide similar stability while allowing for broader frequency coverage, although this incurs a processing cost. In general, stabilizing antenna gains using complex algorithms reduces variability, but only up to a certain point, after which further improvements become negligible due to processing overhead. In addition, we found that antenna gain stabilization has diminishing effects beyond a certain radius from the array's central path. Finally, we discussed how combining redundant data can impact the reliability of antenna gain stabilization in practice. Our findings will inform the design and strategy for frequency and spectral analysis tools at NOEMA and other large arrays, as well as the data processing required to utilize their full capabilities. In particular, we recommend adopting a dual-approach processing scheme that prioritizes analyzing channels in real-time and wide bands offline, while also providing options for channel-based offline analysis and wide band-based real-time processing. In terms of data rates, we estimate that NOEMA will require approximately 1.6 gigabits per second to accommodate real-time processing of all its frequency channels and real-time correlation. In addition, we found that the amount of data storage required to process all its frequency channels in offline mode would be approximately 6 terabytes per hour, while real-time data storage needs would be significantly lower, at approximately 60 megabits per second. Recent developments in analyzing complex network structures lead to the introduction of tensor join as a novel operation between tensors and matrices. This concept has great potential in examining the spectral properties of weighted hypergraphs, which are a natural extension of simple graphs with more expressive structures. Joining a tensor and a matrix yields a higher-order tensor, enabling the creation of a positive semidefinite matrix from this tensor. This new method offers flexibility in creating positive semidefinite matrices and provides a dual approach to previous methods. The application of tensor join in generating positive semidefinite matrices enables the use of semidefinite programming and convex relaxation techniques. To illustrate its effectiveness, we use tensor join to derive conditions for the existence of nontrivial eigenvalues in hypergraphs and to develop a spectral hypergraph partitioning algorithm. The results demonstrate that tensor join outperforms its matrix join counterpart in terms of partitioning quality and runtime efficiency. Additionally, tensor join enables the derivation of more accurate and stricter bounds for the second-largest eigenvalue of hypergraphs. The findings from this research can be adapted to analyze the stability of weighted hypergraphs within the context of bipartite networks and database design. The methods described here are applicable to simple graphs as well, which is evident in our experiments. The methods described here are implemented in the open-source library HypergraphX, which is available at https://github.com/tyz2015/HypergraphX. In the analysis of continuous outcomes in clinical trials, untransformed data is often treated as though it follows a normal distribution with a single mean value, despite that being an unlikely scenario in real-world research. The standard method for analyzing untransformed data, which involves fitting a normal distribution even when data points do not follow that pattern, can result in overly optimistic confidence intervals. We present an alternative approach that involves fitting a normal distribution with varying mean values over discrete intervals of the data, using a particular type of function tailored to short data series. The method described here is particularly suited to clinical trials with short data series, making it well-suited to scenarios where time or sequence of measurement is the variable that the mean of the data is being conditioned on. A new approach to identifying reaction pathways has been developed, drawing on concepts from lattice Monte Carlo methods and nonequilibrium dynamics. This approach, called conformational space annealing, involves initializing simulations with highly unstable configurations and gradually relaxing constraints to produce reactive conformations. A dynamic potential energy landscape (PEL) analysis tool allows for the creation of reaction pathways that are stable under nonequilibrium conditions, yielding more accurate results than equilibrium-based approaches. This method has been applied to the reactions of isomerizing propanediene and crossing from propene oxide monomer to cyclohexene monomer, producing distinct pathway profiles that are not obtainable via equilibrium PEL analysis. A key aspect of this approach is the production of parametric reaction pathway surfaces that can inform metadynamics simulations and guide explorations of reaction mechanisms. Furthermore, the pathway profiles obtained via nonequilibrium PEL analysis provide insight into kinetic phenomena, such as transition barrier shifts, that are absent at equilibrium. Overall, the combination of nonequilibrium pathway approaches and dynamic PEL analysis offers a powerful means of understanding both equilibrium and nonequilibrium chemical phenomena. These approaches are expected to yield more accurate predictions of reaction rates and pathways, ultimately facilitating a deeper understanding of the role of dynamics in shaping both equilibrium and nonequilibrium chemical properties. In 2019, researchers $\textit{K.}$ $\textit{Mikkola}$ and $\textit{P.}$ $\textit{Pikkala}$ introduced a specific type of topology for almost Hull-kernel-type topology on the lattice of subgroups, denoted as $\mathfrak{A}NK$, which is associated with normal subgroups. They later generalized this concept to other types of topological lattices. This current research revisits and extends the almost Hull-kernel-type topology to other lattice structures while exploring additional mathematical properties. Our study focuses on the separation axioms, compactness, connectedness, the properties of specific types of filters and ideals within $\mathfrak{A}NK$. Additionally, the paper investigates the properties of Hausdorff, regular, and Urysohn spaces in relation to $\mathfrak{A}NK$. Similar investigations are also conducted for $\mathfrak{A}F$, which is defined as the lattice of normal subgroups of a group modulo its finite subgroups. Our research explores the interplay between the various properties of these group structures and their corresponding topologies, which contributes to a deeper understanding of the mathematical properties. Our findings suggest that the most suitable group structure for exploring the topological properties of $\mathfrak{A}NK$ and $\mathfrak{A}F$ is the Hausdorff space. Our study also demonstrates that $\mathfrak{A}NK$ and $\mathfrak{A}F$ exhibit the properties of regular spaces and resolvable spaces when considered as Hausdorff spaces. Our research further shows that the connectedness property of $\mathfrak{A}NK$ and $\mathfrak{A}F$ depends on the group structure. To conclude, the paper provides a comprehensive overview of the various properties explored in the study. Our research is the first of its kind in the field of group theory, offering insights into the topological properties of the lattice of subgroups. Our findings are validated by numerous examples and counterexamples presented in the study. Our research is a foundation for further exploring the topological properties of the lattice of subgroups of a group. The derivation of equations governing adiabatic moist-air dynamics is often hindered by the need to establish spatial and temporal distributions for water vapor saturation. In the past, approximations such as the $\delta$-method have been used, but these have drawbacks like decreasing accuracy as the solution changes. In this research, we focus on the steady-state solution and use a specific value, $\kappa$, for all calculations. This leads to the creation of a simplified equation, which is a modified version of the original equation. By testing this new equation, we find that it produces results for atmospheric heights that are 10 to 100 times greater than those achieved with the $\kappa$-average. Additionally, the modified equation allows for the incorporation of larger areas of super-saturation and enhances the accuracy of numerical simulations. This new equation is beneficial for the simulation of long-term processes and large-scale systems where the precise tracking of water vapor concentrations is essential. As such, it is applicable for the study of atmospheric dynamics on very large scales, such as over the Earth's surface. It is less suitable, however, for processes on smaller scales and for short-term, localized events. Furthermore, we use the Poisson equation to show that the necessary conditions for the emergence of periodic behavior in adiabatic systems with moist air are met. This confirms the possibility of periodic behavior in such systems and highlights the importance of incorporating dynamic equations for condensation. Overall, this new equation enhances our understanding of adiabatic dynamics and facilitates the exploration of larger-scale systems. It also provides a foundation for future research into long-term processes and large-scale systems. Furthermore, we find that the essential features of the equation are preserved even when we incorporate more complex equations for water vapor transport. As such, it is a valuable tool for the simulation and study of atmospheric dynamics on very large scales. Research into disruptions in Advanced Tokamaks, such as those found in WEST, has focused on understanding the birth and death of Palm Tree Modes (PTMs). These modes develop from Edge-Localized Modes (ELMs) and magnetic islands as they grow, influencing the disruption phenomenology. A study has been conducted to investigate how PTMs grow and impact the disruption process. The research analyzed disruptions from WEST experiments through the NIMROD MAST2000 equilibrium code, exploring the impact of PTMs and their connection to disruption behavior. It considered various scenarios: PTMs originating from growing magnetic islands during ELMs, PTMs born from unstable Free Boundary modes, and PTMs born from unstable Deep Interior MHD modes. The research examined the impact of these PTMs on disruption behavior, focusing on their numerical simulation as free boundary modes, and incorporated PTMs into the NIMROD code to analyze their effect on the disruption. The results of the simulations showed that PTMs born from magnetic islands and Deep Interior MHD modes have a limited impact on the disruption, whereas PTMs born from free boundary modes have a significant effect on the disruption, leading to shorter e-folding times for PTMs and shorter disruption times for Deep Interior MHD modes compared to non-PTM scenarios. Additionally, the research found that PTMs born from Deep Interior MHD modes lead to slower PTM growth and a longer disruption for PTMs born from magnetic islands compared to non-PTM scenarios. The research demonstrates that PTMs born from magnetic islands and Deep Interior MHD modes do not significantly impact the disruption, whereas PTMs born from free boundary modes have a substantial effect on the disruption. The research also shows that PTMs born from Deep Interior MHD modes and magnetic islands exhibit slower growth and a longer disruption compared to non-PTM scenarios. Research on detecting hate speech has typically focused on technical and linguistic aspects, but overlooked the potential of socio-cultural context, despite its crucial role in understanding the 'other' in online discourse. Our study investigates how socio-cultural context is perceived by humans and machine learning models, by examining its representativeness in training data and relevance in prediction outcomes. The lack of socio-cultural context in training data and the limited accuracy of machine learning models when applied to hate speech detection tasks on under-resourced languages, such as Yoruba, was also discovered. Our analysis suggests that underutilized African languages, like Yoruba, pose a significant challenge to machine learning models in hate speech detection. The findings imply that training data should be enriched with socio-cultural context and more effective algorithms need to be developed to tackle the issue. The behavior of large neuronal networks connected by gap junctions can be studied using a mean-field approximation when networks are randomly connected. This method allows for the analysis of collective oscillations in networks composed of neurons with different time constants and widths of degree distribution. By examining degree distributions of varying widths (from bornheimer to Poisson), our analysis has shown that the width significantly impacts the frequency of collective oscillations. Additionally, our results indicate a strong relationship between the time constants of neurons and the type of collective oscillations that emerge, whether they be high-frequency (large degree, bornheimer distribution) or low-frequency (Poisson distribution). This work provides valuable insight into neuronal networks, offering a practical consideration for experimental designers to take into account. Furthermore, our results provide a foundation for exploring additional factors such as heterogeneity in time constants and node dynamics. Lastly, this research is relevant to non-neuronal fields as well, providing a framework for analyzing collective behavior in systems of coupled elements. Collective oscillations in networks of coupled elements can be observed in mechanical systems, discussed in [1], as well as in biological systems, discussed in [2]. The mathematical framework developed in this study could be applied to understanding collective oscillations in a broader range of coupled systems. Researchers have long sought to utilize neural networks to automatically repair bugs in code. A novel technique is introduced in this study, specifically designed for bugs related to method API misuse, with the aim of closing a critical gap in the field. A deep network is employed to directly generate a bug fix based on a given input test case, without the need for a previous, related bug in the database. In preliminary evaluations, the system demonstrated impressive results, accurately replicing 91% of human fixes in one dataset and exceeding human performance in another. Following further analysis, the system was refined and ultimately evaluated on two additional datasets, yielding results that rival the best previous methods. A significant finding is that the system's preliminary performance was not due to matching previous bug fixes exactly; instead, it appears that many human fixes were initially targeted with the same repair strategy, highlighting the effectiveness of the proposed approach and the potential for improving bug fixing with more sophisticated networks. Detailed human evaluation of the system's performance also revealed that the system-generated fixes shared similar characteristics to those provided by humans, including new code snippets, modified test cases, and code words. A new dataset was also introduced, containing 1,600 method misuse bug reports from two open-source software systems, providing a resource for further research in the field. Based on performance metrics, the system's performance can be characterized as solid, steady, and robust. Analysis of the system's performance also highlighted interesting patterns in the relationships between its parameters and performance metrics. A new version of the system's architecture and associated training data is available at https://github.com/employ-ai/employ-bug-repair. Teacher-student knowledge transfer has emerged as a crucial pre-training method for fine-tuning. The process involves initially training a strong model (the teacher) on a large dataset, then utilizing it to expedite the training of a weaker model (the student) on a smaller dataset. Although training the student directly from the teacher is often hindered by performance gaps and computational disparities, we propose a novel approach to tackle these challenges. This paper draws a parallel between teacher-student knowledge transfer and channel pruning, a compression technique that enables the student to learn in the teacher's domain by eliminating unnecessary teacher channels and matching the teacher's configuration with student channels. We develop two strategies, Teacher Channel Pruning Compression (TCPC) and Knowledge Channel Pruning Compression (KCPC), that integrate channel pruning with knowledge transfer. By first pruning the teacher, TCPC allows the student to learn in the teacher's domain by eliminating unnecessary teacher channels, while KCPC enables the student to learn with knowledge from the teacher's pruned channels, thereby leveraging the teacher's knowledge while avoiding performance degradation. Our experiments on various datasets demonstrate the superiority of our proposed methods in compared to existing state-of-the-art compression techniques and transfer learning methods. Ultimately, we found that our techniques successfully transformed the teacher-student knowledge transfer process, enabling the student to learn efficiently from the teacher. The source code for our proposed approach can be found at https://github.com/ghoul-2020/TCPC-KCPC. Auction designers strive to create mechanisms where the revenue generated from selling multiple items is the same as selling those items separately. However, separate sales are optimal for many demand structures, and there is no universally applicable mechanism that achieves this, except for two-payment mechanisms in certain scenarios. We investigate the largest class of revenue functions that can be achieved through standalone mechanisms, and reveal that the mechanism behind second-price auctions is the only one among six examined mechanisms that yields this class regardless of the demand structure. However, a growing trend in the field suggests that teaching models to estimate 3D scene geometry might be a more effective way forward.  This paper explores the benefits of incorporating a module that predicts scenes and their viewpoints in a global coordinate system, using classification as a fallback option when needed.  Key to this method is how the training loss is designed - opting for a reconstruction-based loss on 2D images leads to better results, whereas a corresponding loss on 2D classification labels yields underperformance.  Moreover, using geometry prediction over image classification reduces the negative impact of noise in the training set on pre-training representations.  Geometric features derived from scenes that demand more accurate 3D reconstruction, such as those containing distant objects or narrow viewpoints, tend to be more valuable than their counterparts in easy scenes.  A thorough analysis via ablation studies confirms that the proposed training approach enhances the quality of learned representations and facilitates downstream tasks like object detection.  Incorporating this method into a pre-trained model used for image classification yields improvements of up to 3.4% in performance on the Linthicum dataset and 3.2% on the PASCAL VOC 2007 dataset.  A related codebase for this work can be found at https://github.com/asharakeh/GeometricVision. Our investigation reveals that using the narrow width approximation for top quark decay leads to inaccuracies when analyzing certain matrix element processes, resulting in distorted outcomes. To address this, a modified calculation method is introduced, which accounts for both the top quark's finite width and its impact on phase space constraints. By comparing the standard and modified methods, a comprehensive assessment is conducted to evaluate their relative accuracies in calculating differential distributions. The results suggest that the modified method provides a more accurate analysis, exhibiting agreement with Monte Carlo simulations at a margin of less than 1% in most cases. However, the accuracy of both methods is found to be significantly affected by the choice of kinematic variables, particularly those associated with the top quark's decay products. In contrast, better agreement is observed when analyzing variables linked to the original proton-proton collision, though with slightly larger discrepancies. The study highlights the importance of considering the top quark's width when analyzing differential distributions and suggests that standard methods may introduce inaccuracies in certain situations, justifying the need for an alternative, more precise analysis. Autonomous driving systems, especially those using sensors, often face partially observable situations, such as navigating a winding road where a driver may see several hundred meters ahead but a robot may see only a few meters. Recurrent Neural Networks, popular in deep learning applications, have been observed to excel in such hidden Markov models by using past information to predict the present state. Past work has demonstrated the effectiveness of RNN cells, such as the LSTM and GRU, in solving the hidden Markov learning problem, often surpassing fully observable scenarios and approaching optimal levels of performance. Notably, researchers found that these RNN cells performed best when implemented as part of a feedforward network rather than a fully connected architecture. Building on this insight, our team modified the RNN cell layer in a feedforward network to solve the hidden Markov learning problem and achieved near-optimal performance, supporting the idea that RNN cells encode past information in this context. Additionally, our results indicate that these encoders can be found through reinforcement learning methods. The modified network also demonstrated the ability to learn in scenarios with multiple hidden states, such as the linear bandit problem. Overall, our results provide empirical evidence for how RNN cells encode past information and offer insights into their use in deep learning applications. They also highlight the potential for further research into the properties of RNN cells, such as their ability to learn in partially observable scenarios and their utility in autonomous driving systems and other related tasks. This is achieved through a memory component designed to store and process logical values rather than raw intermediate outputs. A common challenge in image processing and restoration involves removing image blur caused by factors such as atmospheric disturbance, sensor limitations, or motion error in imaging systems. In this study, we explore the specific challenge of deblurring satellite images, which can be affected by various types of noise and distortion. To address this task, we employ a deep learning strategy using a novel approach for regulating the structure of the blur kernel and a conditional Wasserstein GAN with a Gausson loss function. Our results demonstrate the efficacy of our model through extensive testing on synthetic data and a large-scale dataset derived from commercial satellites suffering from motion error, which we make available to the research community for training and validation purposes. Our findings indicate that our model significantly outperforms a state-of-the-art low-level restoration method and a highly advanced deep learning super-resolution approach on the same dataset. Additionally, we have developed a web-based interactive tool for researchers to replicate our work and contribute to the field. This paper develops the theory of Rota-Baxter maps in the context of (BiHom)pre-Lie modules. Building on this introduction, it establishes connections between Rota-Baxter (BiHom)pre-Lie modules and (BiHom)pre-Lie algebras, as well as the relationships between integral-type Rota-Baxter (BiHom)pre-Lie modules and Lie modules. Furthermore, it demonstrates how (BiHom)pre-Lie modules can be created from Rota-Baxter (BiHom)paired modules and how integral-type (BiHom)pre-Lie modules can be constructed from Lie modules. These findings allow for the creation of (BiHom)integral Rota-Baxter modules derived from (BiHom)integral modules. Ultimately, it is shown that the categories of Rota-Baxter (BiHom)pre-Lie modules and (BiHom)Lie modules correspond to the Schur representations of the Steenrod algebra when certain conditions are met. The study then generalizes its results to the BiDGLA setting, enabling the determination of colimits of Rota-Baxter maps in the BiHompre-Lie setting. These findings are ultimately used to establish the definition of BiHomcolored Rota-Baxter operators within the BiHompre-Lie setting. Lastly, it is demonstrated how the BiHomcolored Rota-Baxter operators of Baxter and integral types can be generated from those of Rota-Baxter and integral types in the BiHommodule setting. The study's findings are anticipated to expand the scope of its theory and provide a foundation for further research in the field. The corresponding authors, Xiaofeng Li and Li Guo, are primarily responsible for the work included in this paper. This paper explores the potential of using natural language assertions to validate imperative programs through formal verification. We demonstrate this capability by developing a verification engine that translates the assertions in Z notations to F- Z specification and matches them with assumptions or postconditions in the specification. Our engine is integrated into the Z proof assistant tool. For each Z specification and target program, the proof assistant searches for a matching F- Z abstract state machine. If a match is found, then the target program satisfies the given specification. Otherwise, the proof assistant identifies the sub-expressions on both sides of the specification that differ and highlights the discrepancies. This research also provides guidance on translating high-level program annotations into F- Z specification and transforming target program implementations for abstract state machines. We apply our approach to the verification of several programs, including a banking system, a counter, and a stack. The results show that our tool successfully verifies the banking system and the counter but identifies inconsistencies between the stack specification and target program. The failure leads to the presentation of several possible interpretations of the sub-expressions on both sides of the specification difference. Canopus is a distributed data storage protocol that allows multiple servers to collaborate and pretend a single, highly available storage system exists. Each server in a Canopus setup stores files but also designates a primary peer to manage the system, with the rest acting as backups. If a primary server fails, the next highest server takes over, but this incurs a time delay and the need for manual configuration. Our enhanced protocol, RCanopus, integrates smoothly with existing storage systems and seamlessly adapts to server failures, preserving data integrity with minimal exceptions. RCanopus tests show that it outperforms Canopus in most scenarios, especially when failures occur, restoring full functionality in under 300 microseconds. RCanopus was successfully tested against over 30 failure scenarios without data loss, thanks to its robust design. Our performance comparisons across eight servers reveal that RCanopus matches the speed of standalone storage, outperforming Canopus across multiple benchmarks, including a 25% speed boost over fibre channel. RCanopus demonstrates resilience not just in server failures but also in the event of network separation, and we show that it retains data integrity in rare instances of storage media failure. Our comprehensive evaluation of RCanopus demonstrates its reliability and efficiency in managing distributed storage, making it an ideal choice for applications requiring high-speed data transfer, such as virtual machines and databases. RCanopus is designed to be compatible with existing storage systems, at the moment only tested on iSCSI but also compatible with block-level systems like NVMe/OF. Our protocol is open-source and available for public use at the link provided. Object detection has become a cornerstone of modern computer vision, with deep learning methods having achieved impressive performance in recent years. However, these methods often underestimate uncertainty or overlook it altogether. We introduce BayesOD, an object detection framework based on Bayesian networks, that naturally incorporates uncertainty by utilizing an object-oriented Bayesian algorithm. BayesOD comprises an object detector backbone, an object classifier, and an object finder, all designed to work in tandem. Notably, BayesOD generates uncertainty estimates that closely mirror the observed distribution, as demonstrated through rigorous performance testing on PASCAL VOC and COCO datasets. BayesOD outperforms existing uncertainty estimation methods while maintaining competitive detection accuracy, with its source code freely accessible at https://github.com/zechser/bayesod. Our results suggest that uncertainty estimates derived from BayesOD exhibit superior fidelity compared to other approaches. We also examine various prediction behaviors exhibited by BayesOD, encompassing conservative and aggressive uncertainty-assigned predictions, with implications for assessment of model reliability in real-world applications. Our analysis highlights potential applications of BayesOD in diverse scenarios, such as predictive maintenance and data mining, where robust uncertainty estimates are paramount. Ultimately, BayesOD represents a promising framework for object detection under uncertainty, with its inherent modularity allowing for seamless integration with existing object detectors. By leveraging an object-oriented Bayesian algorithm, BayesOD achieves accurate uncertainty estimates while maintaining detection performance comparable to non-Bayesian methods, thus serving as a suitable baseline for various applications. A reliable hippocampus segmentation method is crucial for both clinical and research purposes, particularly in evaluating patients with post-surgical resections due to epilepsy. We developed an open-source, automated method to segment the hippocampus from T1-weighted magnetic resonance images, using a combination of shape-based models and probability maps. When tested on a diverse dataset of non-experts, our method performed better than existing techniques, achieving an average increase of 4-8% in accuracy. Notably, our method demonstrated superior performance when applied to subjects with hippocampus resections, suggesting its high potential for use in patients with post-surgical resections, making it a suitable choice for research and treatment evaluations. The code for our method is freely available online. 

Key phrases: hippocampus segmentation, shape-based models, automated method, post-surgical resections, epilepsy research.
