We analyzed the prevalence of tidal features in early-type galaxies using a substantial sample from a combination of two primary catalogues. These tidal features are thought to be the result of interactions with companion galaxies. Our analysis involved the GASS dataset and the Kauffmann ETG catalogue, yielding a diverse sample of 661,533 galaxies with a broad mass range of approximately $10^{9}-10^{13}$ solar masses, spanning redshifts from 0.02 to 0.15. We calculated the fraction of tidal features present in these galaxies as a function of mass and other factors. Our results show that tidal features are more common in lower-mass galaxies and less common in higher-mass galaxies, with a notable exception above $10^{11}$ solar masses. We also found that tidal features are more likely to be oriented at a perpendicular angle to the galaxy's major axis. Additionally, we observed that tidal features are more likely to be located near the galaxy's center, but substructure can be found in nearly a quarter of these galaxies. Our research implies that interactions with companion galaxies can lead to the development of central tidal features and spiral structure in lower-mass galaxies. However, the existence of tidal features in higher-mass galaxies challenges this theory, suggesting that alternative mechanisms such as minor mergers or gas stripping may be at play. Future studies could utilize simulations to further explore the dynamics of tidal features and help validate our findings. Our research provides a foundation for the development of a machine learning model to identify tidal features automatically. We propose that further research into the characteristics of tidal features is crucial to understanding their origins. The study of fast radio bursts, particularly their polarization properties, has significantly advanced in recent years. Most FRBs, except for those caused by giant pulses from pulsars, tend to have complex polarization patterns that observers encounter less frequently in comparison to pulses from individual sources. Theoretical models explaining the FRB emission can be narrowed down with the aid of multifrequency, polarimetric observations. To test various emission models, researchers analyzed four FRBs, FRB 121102, FRB 180418 and two other bursts, incorporating single-channel and multi-frequency data. The former increased the likelihood of observing polarized emission, while the latter allowed constraints to be placed on the emission models. The findings suggest that FRB 121102's radio emission likely originates from an incoherent scatterszoo scenario, whereas FRB 180418's radiomodel appears more plausible for FRB 180729 and FRB 201004. The research demonstrates the value of multifrequency, polarimetric observations in constraining FRB emission models. Furthermore, the scatterszoo model may provide a framework for interpreting the recently discovered, highly polarized FRB 202026. The scatterszoo model, supported by FRB 121102 and FRB 202026, suggests that the circular polarization observed in these bursts arises from the Faraday rotation measure. The increasing power of laser systems necessitates precise modeling to prevent damage, which poses a technical challenge due to their intricate optical designs and the need to consider multiple beam interactions when modeling them. This difficulty is compounded by the need to apply complex physical processes, such as dispersion and diffraction, in the context of time-dependent photochemical reactions. Our work presents the first public release of ZYTO, a software platform developed using Python that facilitates the simulation and analysis of high-power CPA and nonlinear laser systems. The ZYTO software platform incorporates modules for specifying nonlinear interactions, managing data, and generating plots, all within a modular structure that allows for easy extension and customization. The platform is complemented by a comprehensive Python library, called ZL, which provides classes and functions for addressing various laser system simulation needs. In this paper, we provide an overview of the ZYTO software platform and ZL library, accompanied by example descriptions highlighting their respective features. The ZYTO software platform, along with the associated documentation and example descriptions, is publicly available for download on the GitHub platform. The public release of the ZYTO software is intended to contribute to the development of accurate models for high-power laser systems, promote collaboration, and support research in photochemical and nonlinear laser schemes. The accuracy and performance of the ZYTO software platform were verified by comparing numerical solutions of the nonlinear laser system with experimental data. The platform's capabilities can be utilized in a variety of scientific and engineering applications, encompassing studies in biomedical photochemical reactions, laser material processing, and nonlinear interactions, among others. The public release of the ZYTO software platform is accompanied by a call for collaboration, with the aim of extending its capabilities to related scientific and engineering disciplines, particularly in biomedical and chemical reactions, with a possible future public release of advanced extensions and customized versions. We introduce a pioneering framework that leverages pre-trained models paired with
partially annotated data, circumventing the necessity for comprehensive, human-driven
annotation in the generative model domain. Comprising two core components - a
unsupervised pre-training stage and a fine-tuning mechanism - our approach can be
applied universally to any model design. In a demonstration of its efficacy, we
apply our framework to two distinct problems: density estimation and action recognition. 
In the former case, we utilize a partially annotated dataset to generate complete
density functions of unlabeled data, achieving superior results over action zero-shot
learning techniques, including Deep Action Residual Network. In the latter instance,
we develop a novel unsupervised pre-training strategy for Deep Action Residual Network
and Deep Kinematics Network, and through zero-shot learning experiments on UCF101 and
HMBDB datasets, we establish an unprecedented standard of performance, outdoing
previous methods such as Deep Fisher-Buchman Attention and Deep Action Transformer. 
In addition to these outcomes, we make available our framework and related code for
public use. Publicly accessible at: https://github.com/ghmzss/zero-shot-action-rec/tree/master. 
This research represents a significant advancement in the generative model field,
especially for the action recognition domain, through its innovative use of partially
annotated data for model initialization. In a related paper, we discuss how our work
can be applied to a new domain, i.e.  semantic segmentation, and present our research
in ICCV 2019 and CVPR 2019, and won the best paper award in the former conference.

We've investigated three variants of slice sampling, namely hit-and-run, whitened slice sampling, and their combination, to determine their efficiency in accepting non-zero proposals. Our findings suggest whitened slice sampling accepts around 4-5% non-zero proposals, whereas hit-and-run and its combination yield significantly higher acceptance rates of approximately 40-60% non-zero proposals under certain conditions. Our theoretical analysis explains these results by relating the Koehler-Schmeiser distributions to the accept-reject principle and reveals a connection between the acceptance rates of these distributions. Our findings also suggest that hit-and-run and its combination may propose non-zero values more frequently as the target distribution scales. Notably, our simulations indicate that whitened slice sampling becomes comparable to hit-and-run and its combination in terms of efficiency when targeting well-conditioned distributions. Furthermore, our combined approach outperforms whitened slice sampling in terms of efficiency and may be used as an alternative to hit-and-run, particularly when sampling from non-normal distributions, as the former accepts proposals only if they meet specific criteria. While some prior methods segmented the brain and spinal cord as a single unit, others treated them as separate objects without considering their physical connection. We developed a novel, semi-automated technique that utilizes a T1-weighted MRI dataset to segment both the brain and spinal cord based on prior knowledge of their physical relationship. Our method employs Gaussian Processes to create models for the brain and spinal cord based on training data, and these models are used to generate predictions based on the T1-weighted images. Our approach also includes a fusion step that enhances the accuracy of the spinal cord segmentation. We evaluated our method on the MICCAI 2019 AD neuropathology prediction challenge dataset consisting of 402 subjects and compared it with existing state-of-the-art methods. The results showed that our method outperformed others in segmentation accuracy, and the predicted volumes correlated well with post-mortem measures, and also demonstrated a moderate correlation with the estimated atrophy volume in Alzheimer's Disease patients. The developed method has the potential to contribute to the study of Alzheimer's Disease progression by providing accurate segmentation of the brain and spinal cord volumes. In the field of deep neural networks and visual retrieval, the effectiveness of triplet loss in image ranking and retrieval has been well-established, with most current methods focusing on directly minimizing triplet loss to achieve retrieval performance. However, when analyzing the gradient of triplet loss, we noticed that its three components are not equally affected, with the direction of their gradients differing significantly. Based on this insight, we developed a new method, direction-aware triplet loss, to decompose the pair-wise loss gradient into its direction and magnitude to adaptively adjust the learning process. Theoretical evidence shows that minimizing the direction component contributes significantly to improving the model's performance, while experiments on various datasets demonstrate that our method yields better results, is more robust, and can even eliminate the impact of hard samples, requiring fewer gradients to compute compared to previous methods, thus resulting in a notable decrease in computational cost. The method has been found to be particularly effective in large-scale image retrieval tasks, yielding performance improvements of up to 9% over current state-of-the-art methods. The concept of $R_\infty$-nilpotency in a group refers to the largest possible nilpotency level that can be achieved by taking the $\infty$-factor of the group's norm, a significant idea introduced by Tweddle in 1922 and further developed by Alahmadi and Noor in 2019. In this paper, we explore some key properties related to $R_\infty$-nilpotency and examine the connection between this concept and the endoproduct operation. We provide endoproduct representations that result in nilpotent groups and generalize a finding by Tweddle on the endoproduct of two finite groups. We also identify the endoproduct nilpotency limit for any group and establish the existence and characteristics of a non-nilpotent endoproduct for non-Abelian groups. Furthermore, we prove that there is no universal endoproduct limit independent of the chosen group. In addition, we explore how $R_\infty$-nilpotency influences the properties of finite 2-group exponents and examine the endoproduct exponent limitations for these groups. We also develop a database of 34 finite 2-group exponents and examine the implications of our findings in relation to the work by Noor in 2020. Lastly, we investigate the connection between $R_\infty$-nilpotency and the endoproduct of Abelian and non-Abelian p-groups, identifying both nilpotent and non-nilpotent examples to characterize the endoproduct exponent properties for these groups. To address these difficulties, we've developed a novel inversion method that employs an adaptive strategy to efficiently refine the parameter search space. This approach is versatile and can be easily extended to accommodate diverse numerical schemes and data types. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method in two distinct scenarios: a model one-dimensional system to illustrate its performance in low-noise scenarios, and a nonlinear two-dimensional system to showcase its ability to handle noisy data, and compare its results with those obtained using alternative schemes. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive open-source code to facilitate its application in different fields. Ultrafast experiments play a crucial role in various disciplines, and our method aims to contribute to advancements in time-resolved spectroscopy, diffractive imaging, and other techniques. This work is freely available at teno.squezga.in.

The COVID-19 pandemic has brought contact tracing into the digital age, resulting in a global rollout of various contact tracing apps and centralised tracing systems across governments, driven by a mix of motivations, including both good intentions and concerns for national security and public order. Faced with the trade-offs between individual privacy, collective surveillance, and public health, different societies have made disparate choices, leading to a complex landscape where contact tracing is now embedded in daily life, yet also a source of anxiety, mistrust, and resistance. This article explores the social implications of contact tracing in Brazil, Germany, and India - countries at different stages of development, with distinct healthcare systems, and unique societal approaches to tracing - highlighting how contact tracing has impacted daily life, influenced public perception, and shaped resistance to the tracing effort. Ultimately, our research reveals that contact tracing has become a polarising issue, exposing deep societal divisions and raising questions about the long-term consequences for individual freedom and collective public health. The introduction of Signal PINs as an additional authentication step in the Signal app has been met with concerns about security due to user-chosen passwords. Researchers have explored ways to guess these PINs, while the Signal team has been tight-lipped about the details. In our study, we conducted an experiment to understand how typical users select Signal PINs, and found that most choose simple, easy-to-remember numbers that reflect their personal identity. We found that 71% of participants' Signal PINs are 4 digits or less in length and 56% start with the first digit of their phone's keypad. Our survey also revealed that users prioritize convenience and ease when creating PINs, rather than making them secure. Given that Signal PINs are meant to enhance security, we recommend that users choose complex passwords and prioritize security over convenience. Our research has implications for other authentication systems, and suggests that educating users about the purpose of authentication is crucial for better security practices. In particular, we found that users who understood the reason for their PIN chose more complex passwords and employed better security practices. In light of this, we suggest integrating educational content within the authentication process to improve security. Ultimately, we believe that integrating PINs with biometric authentication, such as fingerprint or face recognition, would be a more secure option. These rules are expressed as Chebyshev series and, at a given precision, require less summand evaluation than their non-solar counterparts, which makes them more suitable for solar energy applications where numerous integrals need to be computed. The proposed quadrature rules are particularly useful for scenarios with small field-of-view angles and high precision requirements. They are also suitable for scenarios involving scattered radiation that needs to be multiplied by the solar collectance function or the scattered phase function. An alternative variant of the solar-weighted quadrature rules is provided, which can be used in scenarios with positive summands by converting the Chebyshev series to Fourier-Chebyshev series. This allows the utilization of fast Fourier transform techniques for efficient evaluation. The new solar-weighted quadrature rules are validated and compared with their non-solar counterparts in both unweighted and weighted quadrature contexts. Our method builds upon the 'textual priming' technique but adapts it to accommodate a mix of human and machine-based input. Utilizing a small set of control instances, fed either manually by humans or generated by machines, we can successfully reduce grammatical gender bias across a range of evaluation metrics. Interestingly, our results indicate that the source of the control instances matters less than the actual process of textual priming itself. Moreover, our findings suggest that the degree of bias reduction achieved by our method varies depending on the specific evaluation metric used. Additionally, our experiments reveal the complexities of bias removal when working with natural language processing models, as removing one type of bias can inadvertently introduce another. Therefore, our approach highlights the need for more sophisticated evaluation metrics that can effectively capture the nuances of human language. Research into the concept of fairness in machine learning has grown, with a focus on evaluating how policies and interventions would impact different groups. Currently, there is a lack of methods that directly assess fairness based on hypothetical scenarios. This research fills this gap by introducing a framework that uses causal inference to evaluate the potential consequences of interventions on model behavior. By applying this framework to a dataset from the U.S. Supreme Court, our method reveals critical fairness issues that could arise from counterfactual policies, such as a potential decrease in accuracy for female decision-makers. This problem highlights the need for methods that balance fairness and efficiency, but our approach highlights the limitations of such methods in practice. By doing so, we underscore the importance of utilizing data-driven techniques to identify and mitigate potential fairness problems that may arise from interventions, counter to current assumptions. This framework also offers the potential for utilization in policy analysis, data-driven fairness assessments, and policy-guided machine learning development. Furthermore, our method can be adapted for the study of other critical social interventions and is relevant to a broad range of domains. The code and dataset used in this research are publicly available. This framework can be expanded to incorporate more complex models, such as neural networks, which would offer significant benefits. Finally, our results emphasize the importance of fairness, accuracy, and the potential consequences of actions on marginalized groups, such as racial minorities and women. By leveraging the tools of causal inference, researchers can gain a deeper understanding of the potential consequences of interventions, which can inform the development of policies and practices to mitigate fairness issues, both in existing and emerging machine learning systems. The direct assessment of fairness based on hypothetical scenarios is a critical area of study, given the far-reaching consequences for marginalized groups, such as racial minorities and women. By utilizing the framework of structural causal models, our method provides a general approach that can be applied to a range of different fairness metrics, such as accuracy, fairness, and other counterfactual properties. The framework of structural causal models offers a versatile tool for the analysis of fairness, accuracy, and other critical aspects, which can be extended to more complex domains. Next-generation radio telescopes, such as the Square Kilometer Array, necessitate local data processing due to massive data transmission requirements.  A cluster of GPUs can potentially meet this need, but developing efficient GPU algorithms poses a significant challenge.  Our research focuses on calculating the coherence of radio astronomy data, with the goal of facilitating real-time image formation and data validation during observations.  Two different approaches for estimating coherence are compared, specifically sampling in time and sampling in bandwidth.  Initial results indicate that bandwidth sampling yields higher signal-to-noise ratios, yet it demands more computational resources.  By leveraging CUDA, we developed two separate GPU algorithms to evaluate these methods and discovered that bandwidth-based coherence is better suited for large-scale radio telescopes due to its greater efficiency while producing similar results.  Furthermore, integrating the coherence estimates into the HOGb software tool allowed us to observe the impact of this step in the imaging pipeline, demonstrating that using coherence estimates from bandwidth sampling yields more accurate results in real-time image formation.  This paves the way for the implementation of bandwidth sampling in large-scale radio telescopes in the future.  Our code is publicly available for review at: https://github.com/astroGPU/coherenceGPU.  This research was supported by the Square Kilometer Array Project and the National Science Foundation (Grant No. 1714621).  A detailed description of the project, including raw data and code, can be found at: https://github.com/astroGPU/phaseIIProposal.  Our team's work on this topic is ongoing and we welcome collaborations, specifically with large-scale radio astronomy infrastructure, to further develop and test our code.  Interested parties can contact us at: [gpu@astro.ucla.edu](mailto:gpu@astro.ucla.edu).  Future work will involve incorporating these methods into the HOGb software tool to facilitate real-time data validation and image formation during observations.  Our goal is to facilitate the adoption of real-time data analysis in radio astronomy, a field in which our coherence estimation algorithm could be applied in other areas of astronomy with similar data transmission constraints.  Future work will also involve exploring the use of our algorithm in astrophysical studies, such as in the analysis of Fast Radio Bursts, and we welcome collaborations to further develop and test our code. Metaphotonics is a rapidly evolving field that combines optical and quantum electrodynamic concepts, relying on light-matter interactions and new physics that emerge from long-lived photonic states. To advance this field, we investigate an all-dielectric nanostructure that exhibits both electric and magnetic resonances when excited with light, allowing these resonances to transmit information and enable complex metasurfaces with various functionalities. By resolving the full electromagnetic response of this nanostructure using analytical and computational methods, we demonstrate its potential implementation in spatial light modulation, near-field coupling at thermal wavelengths, and novel metasurface design at mid-infrared frequencies. This study provides a foundational understanding and introduces new possibilities for future research in metaphotonics, showcasing the unique properties of all-dielectric nanostructures and highlighting their potential to outperform their plasmonic counterparts. Ultimately, we aim to contribute to the development of compact, efficient, and scalable platforms for integrated photonics and nanophotonics. Furthermore, our work serves as a starting point for exploring the intricacies of metaphotonics in the quantum regime, paving the way for applications in quantum information and communication. This research aims to investigate the impact of a movie's star cast on its box office performance, using a dataset of popular Hollywood films from 2012 to 2014. To measure a movie's star power, we consider the average of the actors' recognition ratings. We train a predictive model using a Bayesian Autoencoder, with the goal of accounting for variable star cast selection across different movies. This analysis reveals that a movie's star power is a significant predictor of its revenue, and the Bayesian Autoencoder's prediction accuracy increases when using star cast features. Furthermore, our study reveals that a movie's star power explains only about ten percent of the variance in its revenue, leaving nearly ninety percent unaccounted for. This suggests that there may be more valuable factors to explore for box office prediction, such as a movie's storyline or marketing strategy. To better understand the relationship between star power and revenue, we use a non-parametric density estimator to visualize how a movie's star power influences its revenue, revealing a positive correlation. This relationship holds true across different genres, but is less prominent in genre-specific analysis. This study contributes to the field by (1) providing a more nuanced definition of star power based on recognition ratings, (2) exploring the feasibility of variable selection using a Bayesian Autoencoder, (3) demonstrating the additional explanatory power of star cast features, and (4) offering a simple yet effective prediction model suitable for the entertainment industry. The research also sheds light on the limitations of using star power as a predictor, particularly in specific genres such as action and horror. Ultimately, this study serves as a foundation for further research into the impact of a movie's star cast on its box office performance. Edge CS resides closest to the source of data, handling tasks such as filtering, aggregation, and compression, while core CS focuses on detection, classification, and other higher-level tasks within a distributed or central environment. This dichotomy is essential for ensuring the effective operation of large-scale CP systems. This paper delves into the fundamental principles governing the coexistence of core and edge CS architectures and explores the implications of various configurations, such as core-only, edge-only, and hybrid CP systems. Furthermore, we analyze the computational capabilities of each approach and demonstrate the feasibility of a hybrid architecture using a practical example. This work aims to contribute a deeper understanding of interconnected CP systems. Experiments on two large datasets, MS-COCO and VOC, demonstrate the pseudo-cycle's ability to surpass single-model performance, enhancing Mask R-CNN by 1.4 GPAm$^2$ and 0.8 GPAm$^2$ respectively. Finally, we provide recommendations for future research and development based on the findings of this review. Recent advancements in neural architecture search (NAS) have been hindered by a
critical issue: the lack of a reliable method to eliminate distracting
information from labels, leading to unnecessary computational waste. To
overcome this limitation, this research focuses on developing efficient
abstraction techniques for NAS labels by analyzing their semantic patterns and
interactions. An in-depth analysis was conducted to evaluate current label
cleansing methods, which have been proven ineffective in comparison to the
proposed solutions, namely a transformer-based model fine-tuned with a
knowledge distillation objective and an enhanced transformer model (XT) that
eliminates interference through a multi-head attention-based mechanism. The
results demonstrate that the proposed methods significantly outperform existing
techniques, such as RoBERTa and ELECTRA models, on both the performance of
abstractive labels (average improvement of 8.6% and a peak improvement of 11.4%) 
and the efficiency of NAS experiments (an average reduction in time of 37% with
XT). Two new evaluation metrics, named AUC$_{0.9}$ and AUC$_{0.5}$, were also
introduced to assess the performance of label cleansing methods in the context
of NAS. An open-source tool was shared to facilitate future research in
this area. Our method is adaptable and can be applied to any NAS-based search
algorithm without necessitating modifications. The findings and methodology
were made publicly available at https://github.com/ghmfortuna/labelcleansing
for the purpose of further research and development. Furthermore, this research
also introduces a new label cleansing method, named cleanlabel, that eliminates
noise from labels by capturing their semantic patterns and interactions. The
performance of the cleanlabel method was compared to the xt method on both the
aggregation and fusion phases of the NAS architecture, resulting in a notable
time reduction of up to 37% while maintaining similar performance levels. To
further enhance the efficiency of the NAS architecture, this research also
proposes a new method, named selecton, that eliminates interference from
labels by identifying and focusing on only the relevant, high-confidence cues.
The selecton method is capable of being applied to any NAS-based search
algorithm without requiring modifications. Specifically, this research
demonstrated that selecton combined with the top-k selection method yields a
time reduction of 37% while maintaining similar performance levels on both

To address these issues, we propose a pre-training and fine-tuning approach based on the soup scheme, where a model is pre-trained on multiple domain pairs before being adapted to any target domain. Our method also enables models to better capture task-specific relationships, and demonstrates its effectiveness across semantic segmentation and image classification tasks through experimental results. Further experiments show that our model's performance is relatively robust to hyperparameters and training parameters. A vital area of study has emerged for soft-robotics researchers, focusing on designing flexible robots that mimic living creatures.  To effectively utilize these robots for research, precise control over their movements is necessary.  A key challenge lies in tracking predetermined paths, particularly when interacting with complex environments like soft materials.  A new approach has been developed to improve trajectory tracking of robotic systems interacting with soft substrates, centered around utilizing feedback from force sensors.  By optimizing control based on force feedback, our approach enables more accurate path reproduction, particularly evident in experiments involving a robotic hopper moving on foam.  Notably, the robotic hopper's ability to follow a target path was significantly enhanced, either by adjusting its movement commands directly or by modifying the optimal desired path to compensate for external influences.  Combining this strategy with predictive modeling of robotic behavior has led to successful applications in both robust trajectory tracking and robust feedback generation, demonstrating the potential of our approach to expand the scope of soft-robotics research.  Potential future applications of this technology include human-robot collaboration, medical devices, and other complex soft-robotics scenarios.  Furthermore, the use of soft-robotics feedback control could pave the way for more realistic simulations of complex robotic systems, thereby enhancing performance and accuracy.  Ultimately, our approach may facilitate the development of precise and robust control over a wide range of flexible robots, operating either independently or in conjunction with soft materials. For a spherical domain $D$ of radius $1$ and $l$ equal to a square number, we examine the behavior of the $l$th normalized Steklov eigenvalue, denoted by $\lambda_l (D)$, as the radius increases without bound. This analysis is linked to a problem in shape optimization proposed by Rauch-Barak and Zaltzman in '20, involving the volume-normalized first Steklov eigenvalue. As an alternative, we consider a family of spheres $D_l$ such that $\lambda_l (D_l) = l$, and demonstrate that the volume of $D_l$ tends to a fixed value, regardless of the sphere's axis. This fixed value is in agreement with a separate finding by Rauch-Barak and Zaltzman that the limit of the first eigenvalue's ratio to the sphere's volume, as the radius increases without bound, is a constant. Furthermore, we prove that the given behavior of $\lambda_l (D)$ also occurs when $D$ is replaced by anisotropic shells $D^{\alpha}$, depending on the value of $\alpha \in (0,\infty)$. In such cases, we find that $\lambda_l (D^{\alpha})$ is asymptotically equivalent to $l^2$ as the radius increases without bound. Additionally, we investigate the corresponding minimax formulas for the given eigenvalues and show that, for a fixed $l$, the corresponding extrema are uniformly convergent to our previously calculated values. Finally, we discuss how our findings on Steklov eigenvalues can be applied to a variational problem related to the isoperimetric function introduced by O. Parzani in '95. This problem, which concerns the isoperimetric function on the sphere's surface, is defined as the maximum volume of a spherical cap given a fixed boundary length and radius. We observe that our previous results provide a precise asymptotic behavior for a related function, which is in turn linked to the isoperimetric function itself. In particular, we find that our function's growth rate is uniformly bounded by a linear combination of logarithms and constants. Moreover, we calculate the limiting values of the coefficients in this linear combination, which turns out to be positive for odd numbers and negative for even numbers. Finally, we discuss how our findings can be applied to determine the asymptotic behavior of the isoperimetric function itself. The development of energy models for short-term and long-term planning has become increasingly intertwined, with the latter relying on the former. However, current models with high temporal resolution incur significant expenses due to the infeasibility of generating capacity deployment or expansion in intervals matching real-time operational needs. This paper explores the relationship between temporal resolution and the cost of infeasibility, using the European power system model CORNIX as a case study. By analyzing the costs of infeasibility in STORIX, a stochastic unit commitment tool, and scaling up to hourly intervals, the study demonstrates that the cost of infeasibility peaks at 10-minute intervals, the lowest feasible resolution. Furthermore, the cost of infeasibility is primarily driven by generation capacity costs rather than other factors. Consequently, the study proposes deploying multiple power plants with shorter lead times to facilitate more precise 10-minute-scale generation and operation. Additionally, the study suggests incorporating a flexible optimization module into CORNIX to enable operation at higher temporal resolutions than currently possible. By doing so, the model can better inform the investment in power generation by comparing the costs of infeasibility to other costs associated with corresponding generation capacity deployments or expansions. By reducing infeasibility costs and comparing the outcomes, the module can assist in determining the required number of power plants to be constructed to meet evolving generation needs. Finally, the study indicates that the European Union's Clean Energy Package targets are within reach for new generation investments under decarbonization scenarios, but battery energy storage investments need to be ramped up to meet the package's goals. Nonetheless, the study reveals that the European power system can achieve the same emissions level with fewer new generation investments than predicted, largely due to the overestimation of existing generation capacity limits in the reference scenario. These systems combine public utility and minimal private cost inputs from agents to determine allocations and prices. We demonstrate that ratings influence utility outcomes not only for individual agents but also for the entire market, unlike in Wolpert's original model. Furthermore, we derive analytical solutions in addition to \kappa\-\sistema and \kappa\-\market models to provide a more complete understanding of equilibrium outcomes in Wolpert's \sistema mechanism. Overall, our results reveal that ratings may not always benefit the market but can have a significant impact on individual agents' utilities. To address this, we explore how extending Wolpert's original utility function to include additional function classes could help mitigate the negative consequences of ratings, thereby providing a more versatile framework for understanding and analyzing market behavior. Automated evaluation metrics play a significant role in assessing the performance of summarization systems. Currently available metrics, however, have significant discrepancies between their results and human judgment. In this research, we introduce SummScore, a novel evaluation metric for summarization that is based on the similarity between the distribution of words and their positions of importance. SummScore exhibits minimal variability in human ratings, and its scores are more closely aligned with human judgment compared to existing metrics. Notably, SummScore is particularly effective in evaluating diversity in summaries and its correlation with human judgment is twice as strong as other existing metrics. Furthermore, SummScore is capable of distinguishing summaries between good, bad, and indifferent categories with a high level of performance. Experiments also reveal that SummScore can be used in optimization algorithms to facilitate the development of a better summarization performance criterion. This research builds upon the recent findings regarding recovery of compressively-sensed data that is cross-correlated. To date, most studies in this field have either put forth theoretical frameworks or conducted in-depth analyses of specific methods. In contrast, we have developed an accounting framework that is comprehensive in nature, allowing it to encompass various techniques, such as Basis Pursuit, Soft-Thresholding, and Iteratively-Weighted $\ell_1$. This framework takes into consideration the level of data sparsity, the extent of cross-correlation, and the quantity of available data, offering insights into the limitations and capabilities of different methods under different scenarios. Notably, our framework reveals that, as the amount of cross-correlated data increases, the level of sparsity that can be recovered also increases. This research is available online at arXiv:1902.10399. A related demonstration can be found here. Additionally, a more detailed version of this paper, including supplementary material, is available through arXiv:1902.10399v2. Further investigations into the performance of low-complexity methods, such as greedy algorithms, are presented in arXiv:1408.5494, while an examination of the effectiveness of structured sparsity is detailed in arXiv:1408.6818. A more in-depth discussion of our accounting framework and its application to recovery of compressively-sensed data in the presence of cross-correlation is provided in arXiv:1508.02484. Finally, the use of our accounting framework as a tool for designing cross-correlated compressive imaging systems is explored in arXiv:1609.05057 and demonstrated in a study on compressive imaging of a three-dimensional scene in the presence of cross-correlation in the light intensity values, available online. Our research introduces the BEVFusion framework, a novel two-stage object detection method designed to leverage the strengths of both LiDAR and camera sensors while mitigating their respective weaknesses.  By generating a compact 3D representation from the LiDAR data and mapping it to a predicted 3D map, BEVFusion effectively addresses the LiDAR missing detection issue.  On the second stage,  we establish a camera reference system and introduce a cross-beam focal loss to integrate feature maps with projected 2D heatmaps.  Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing methods, with a significant 2.5 AP box mAP improvement when simulating LiDAR failures, and shows superior robustness in real-world scenarios.  Moreover, our analysis reveals that BEVFusion efficiently reduces car detection errors by 1.1 AP box mAP and 1.6 AP box mAP in urban and highway scenarios respectively when disabling camera input.  The proposed method has been successfully applied to Autoware, a autonomous driving software.  Our code is available at https://github.com/DCS-NUTG/bevfusion. The video can be found at https://youtu.be/8Q8o8o6jw9A.  

Key Contributions:
- Our BEVFusion framework is the first to leverage the cross-beam focal loss to bridge the gap between 2D and 3D projection accurately.
- The method effectively addresses the LiDAR missing detection issue by mapping a predicted 3D map, leading to substantial improvements over previous approaches.
- Our approach exhibits robustness, outperforming existing methods by a substantial margin when simulating sensor failures.
- The method has been successfully applied to Autoware, a autonomous driving software, showcasing its potential for real-world applications.

In this context, we explore the stochastic hydrodynamics equation in a bounded domain, taking into account the influence of external forces as stipulated by Boussinesq. Our primary objective involves calculating the large-scale energy's exponential decay rate under the assumption that the large-scale energy exceeds a critical value. In achieving this goal, we derive a more tractable estimate for the energy's growth, as influenced by the external forces, by applying both local centralizing and compactness methods. Ultimately, we establish that the large-scale energy's behavior, as described by the stochastic hydrodynamics equation, exhibits behaviors characteristic of both conciseness and intermittency, as the large-scale energy approaches a critical value, thereby leading to enhanced dissipation. In order to obtain our estimates, we employ various techniques, including the environment creation method, as well as establishing estimates for the dissipation term in the stochastic Navier-Stokes equation through a novel approach inspired by the work of the renowned mathematician, V. Scheffer in "Principles of a theory for the regular behavior of turbulent flows, as well as the more recent contributions of H. Koch, P. Kronenthal and D. Vellender in 'Dissipation properties of the stochastic Navier-Stokes equation'". Our work culminates in a detailed exploration of the behavior of the stochastic Q-estimate, as derived by the influential mathematician C. DeLellis in his study 'On the regularity of the Trudinger lossless stochastic Navier-Stokes equations', as well as the more recent findings of D. Vellender in his 'Quantitative stochastic hyperbolic compressible system equations in critical space' research, as we demonstrate its influence on the large-scale energy under both conciseness and intermittency conditions. As a final note, we outline potential avenues for future research, as suggested by our findings. The interaction between laser light and a heated fluid is studied under various experimental conditions, with a laser in the visible spectrum being directed at a heated surface in air. As part of this investigation, observations are made of the fluid's thermal expansion and convection, as well as the changes in the laser beam's intensity distribution due to heat and mechanical distortions. These distortions result in complex patterns of light diffraction, which not only depend on the state of the fluid but also on the patterns of scattering produced by the laser itself. It is found that the observed patterns of diffraction are influenced significantly by the fluid's dynamics and the geometric features of the objects present in the area of observation. To better interpret these findings, the theoretical model of a Gaussian laser beam is employed, including the effects of second harmonic generation and Sagnac's self-interference. A notable aspect of this research involves the visual representation of waves in the fluid that, due to their short wavelength, are normally not easily observable, as their detection is facilitated by the response of the laser-diffraction patterns to the fluid's dynamics. Examples are also given of how the observed patterns can serve as indicators of the state of the fluid, as well as potential applications of this research, such as monitoring thermal and mechanical processes or even employing the observed patterns as a form of hidden information storage. Furthermore, the possibility of using an electron microscope to study the behavior of individual molecules and their impact on the fluid's dynamics and the resulting laser-diffraction patterns is explored, as well as the relevance of this research to the study of living organisms and the complex interactions between air, water, and plant or animal matter. Finally, the theoretical model is extended to investigate the behavior of laser-diffraction patterns in the presence of electromagnetic fields, as a means of understanding the response of matter at a quantum level when interacting with laser light. As part of this research, specific examples are given of how the observed patterns can serve as indicators of the presence of electromagnetic fields, as well as potential applications of this theory to the detection and identification of a variety of fields, from the common to the unusual and even paranormal. A brief overview of the research is provided at the end of each chapter, summarizing the main achievements made in the course of this investigation. Ultimately, the research presented in this dissertation aims to contribute meaningfully to our understanding of the complex and intriguing world of light and matter interactions. As an added benefit of this research, specific examples of how the principles explored can be applied to address pressing global issues

The proliferation of IoT devices has generated an immense surge in data streaming, posing significant challenges for processing velocity and massive volumes. Current stream processing technologies are inadequate in managing diverse IoT device telemetry due to limitations in dealing with varying rates, bounded and unbounded data patterns, and dynamic event-time calculations. Moreover, integrating external data and responding to queries asynchronously further complicates the stream processing landscape. To address these shortcomings, we propose H-STREAM, a novel parallel stream processing framework built on hypergraphs for efficient and adaptive management of diverse IoT data streams. H-STREAM effectively leverages hypergraphs to incorporate external data, implement parallelism, and ensure accurate and efficient event-time calculations, thus providing a flexible and robust platform for processing large-scale IoT data streams. The framework also offers a hybrid query layer, enabling asynchronous partial results and facilitating the integration of external knowledge to refine stream queries and enhance overall performance. The effectiveness of H-STREAM is demonstrated through its adaptation to an IoT healthcare platform, providing O(log n) time-to-live capabilities, improved energy efficiency, and reduced communication for wireless sensor nodes, which in turn accelerates the processing of IoT data streams by approximately 2.5 times compared to standard parallel stream processing systems. The hybrid query layer also enables the creation of sophisticated queries on mobile devices with limited resources while streamlining the processing on the server-side. The proposed H-STREAM framework thus presents a robust and efficient solution for managing diverse IoT data streams across various application domains. Accurate cross-section predictions for vector-like quark production rely heavily on the evaluation of non-resonant diagrams, which previously lacked thorough consideration in the literature. We provide an updated analysis of the partial widths and normalization factors for these diagrams, establishing a set of benchmark cases that highlight their significance, particularly at the tree level. We propose a new scale parameterization for the weak interactions of the new vector-like quarks to facilitate a more accurate and standardized comparison between theoretical models and experimental data. We apply this new scale parameterization to the pair production of up-type vector-like quarks at the LHC, taking into account the top quark, Higgs boson, and vector-like quark decays, and calculate the associated partial cross-sections using an automated program. We provide an updated analysis of the total cross-sections for the up-type vector-like quark pair production, accounting for both resonant and non-resonant processes, and compare our results with the partial cross-sections previously calculated by the theoretical community. We establish a set of recommended total cross-sections for the up-type vector-like quark pair production, serving as a unified standard for the vector-like quark research community. We also provide an updated analysis of the LHC sensitivity to the up-type vector-like quark pair production, taking into account the non-resonant decay channel, and discuss the potential for the full cross-section reconstruction at the LHC in the future. Natural language programming has emerged as a research area, focusing on using data mining and machine learning to generate code in response to natural language inputs. Recent studies have made significant progress in this area, particularly for query languages such as SPARQL and SQL. This paper presents a novel approach to generating SPARQL queries utilizing a transformer model with an integrated copy mechanism. This innovation allows the model to copy words directly from the input sentence, thereby addressing potential shortcomings resulting from incomplete models. We evaluated our approach against existing baselines and conducted comprehensive experiments to compare the performance of different models for generating SPARQL queries. The results demonstrate that our proposed model outperforms the others in terms of accuracy, with an impressive 76.59% consistency with human-generated code. Furthermore, we analyzed the relationships between model performance and copy mechanisms, as well as the impact of pre-training datasets on the generated code. The findings suggest that incorporating a copy mechanism enhances the model's ability to produce correct code, particularly when the input sentence fails to convey essential information. Understanding how specific areas of study within Computer Science evolve requires a comprehensive analytical approach. By examining the publication history of relevant conferences and journals, researchers can gain insights into the emergence and growth of distinct fields. Such studies have been conducted in the past by various teams, but a unified database of Computer Science field evolution data has been lacking so far. To address this, we have created a new database, called NMD-CSDL, by combining two existing datasets on conference and journal history. Our findings, however, reveal significant changes in how academic fields have shifted over time, both in how the data is categorized and in the number of fields. To facilitate future research, we have made both our dataset and an updated version of the DOAJ accessible through our website. Additionally, we have shared the code used for data integration and refinement through a public GitHub repository. Our study contributes to the ongoing discussion about how to structurally organize knowledge in Computer Science by analyzing the dynamics of fields and their publications. By doing so, we aim to help inform future structural changes and foster a deeper understanding of the discipline's development. Ultimately, we hope our findings will inform future researchers by providing answers to the following questions: What are the main fields of study in Computer Science? How have these fields evolved over time? How many fields exist, and how many are considered relevant? Our research also raises several questions that we aim to investigate further: What is the optimal number of fields to structurally organize knowledge in Computer Science? How can we improve the analysis of fields by incorporating additional data sources? What is the relationship between fields and the publication venues that contribute to their development? Our findings indicate that incorporating publishing venues into the analysis enhances the quality of the field evolution analysis, but also introduces new challenges. Specifically, we have found that incorporating venues leads to a higher number of fields, increased density, and a lower average clustering compared to previous studies. Our results also reveal that certain fields have emerged, changed, merged, or disappeared over time, and that the development of new fields has slowed in recent years. We have found that the fields that have emerged have tended to be more specialized, and that the development of new fields has been linked to the establishment of new conferences and journals. Our research has also indicated that existing fields have changed over time, and that the number of fields has fluctuated in response to these changes. Although machine learning-based neural network controllers are increasingly used, the lack of effective methods to verify their robustness poses a significant risk. This issue could be addressed by adapting advanced techniques developed for computer vision and machine learning, such as transfer learning, adversarial training, and learning from scratch. These methods can be employed to verify robustness against hypothetical threats and provide a valuable safety net for control systems. Building upon this concept, we present methods to verify robustness that combine theoretical and practical capabilities. Our findings demonstrate that learning from scratch and adversarial training can provide robustness against threats that were not encountered during training, while being computationally efficient. Moreover, we show that these methods can handle complex networks with multiple interconnecting controllers, such as those using reinforcement learning, without computational constraints. Our experimental results using an industrial robot arm as a case study showcase the practical application of these methods to ensure robust neural network control. Ultimately, this research aims to bridge the gap between advanced computer vision and machine learning methods and control theory, providing a valuable contribution to the field. The code and dataset developed for this research are made publicly available. Articulated Neural Rendering (ANR) is an innovative framework that utilizes implicit neural representations to capture dynamic scenes containing multiple moving subjects by scanning a single image. Previous frameworks of this type have been unable to handle complex real-world scenarios due to multiple moving objects. ANR overcomes this limitation by introducing an innovative method for estimating the articulation and pose of moving subjects from a single image. In contrast to previous approaches, ANR can capture subtle articulation details and detect multiple moving subjects per frame. Our results demonstrate significant improvements in accuracy and a significant reduction in reconstruction errors when compared to previous frameworks, as measured by both numerical metrics and visual comparisons. Additionally, ANR achieves new state-of-the-art results on the "NeRF-W" benchmark, a platform that distributes challenging real-world scenes for 3D rendering and tracking. Our source code and trained models are now publicly available.

Artificial intelligence networks excel at detecting objects even when images are heavily distorted, yet humans struggle with the same level of object recognition. To investigate this discrepancy, we developed a visual challenge, 'Object Recognition Under Extreme Transformations,' where participants are presented with an image and asked to identify the object, regardless of its orientation, scale, or shape. Our study revealed that humans can recognize objects despite severe transformations, such as 90-degree rotation, cropping, and blurring, which AI networks fail to withstand. Our findings suggest that objects must be recognizable when rotated by 90 degrees and unscaled, or when at least 60% of their original area remains intact. Interestingly, objects must be at least 16 by 16 pixels in size for humans to identify them. Moreover, our data indicates that objects must be centered within the visual field for humans to recognize them. From our analysis, we derived a set of rules that describe how AI networks fail to recognize objects under certain distortions, which were not previously known. Ultimately, our study sheds light on the limitations of artificial intelligence in visual object recognition and provides a comprehensive understanding of its capabilities compared to human vision. The challenge has been made available as a web browser-based game at our website: http://vision.cogopt.com/ObjectChallenge.html. The database of images used in this study can be accessed through http://vision.cogopt.com/ObjectChallengeDatabase.html. Our work offers a new approach for designing computer vision tasks that mimic human behavior, enabling a more accurate assessment of AI networks, and paving the way for the development of more human-like artificial intelligence. In the online version of federated learning, where devices continuously upload data to a server, the server trains models using this data. Although partial sharing (only transmitting selected data to the server) can reduce participants' communication costs, it also limits the server's ability to make informed model decisions. Asynchronous online federated learning faces an additional challenge in maintaining data privacy due to the accumulation of data across rounds. To address these issues, we propose a two-stage partial sharing method that involves layer-wise quantization and round-based data partitioning. The first approach reduces the size of the server model updates by converting sensitive data to binary, while the second technique splits continuous data into discrete segments based on the server's evolving model accuracy. The proposed communication strategy is paired with a differential privacy framework that incorporates an entropy-based noise injection mechanism to protect participants' data. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through empirical evaluations on binary classification problems using imbalanced datasets. The experimental outcomes show that partial sharing can significantly decrease communication costs while achieving comparable differential privacy levels as would be required if the entire dataset were processed differentially privately. Furthermore, the proposed method ensures that the server model accuracy and generalization performance remain unaffected, outperforming a benchmark baseline that applies differential privacy globally. The proposed partial sharing method thus offers a promising trade-off between communication costs, differential privacy, model generalization, and server training efficiency. In recent years, deep learning-based methods for node representation have emerged, largely focusing on full-supply graphs. These models often struggle with sparse networks, which are prevalent in real-world applications. This paper proposes a novel approach called Sum of Normalized H-order Adjacency Matrix (SNHAM), combining the benefits of the Random Walk (RW) and DeepWalk (DV) methods for node representation in sparse networks. SNHAM leverages the local structure captured by RW and the first-order neighborhood information of DV to produce improved node representations. Experimental results on synthetic and benchmark sparse networks demonstrate SNHAM's superiority over existing node representation learning methods. Furthermore, SNHAM is applied to the task of identifying nodes with high out-degrees in a network, achieving better performance compared to a baseline method. These findings suggest SNHAM as a practical solution for sparse networks. The code for SNHAM is available for download on the repository at https://github.com/Chen-LongYe/SNHAM. Diagnosing mental health disorders often faces challenges in medical practice,
largely due to a lack of reliable, systematic evaluation methods. Traditional
approaches rely on in-depth interviews and observations, which are time-consuming
and may not yield concrete diagnostic results. In recent years, researchers have
explored the potential of using social media data, such as posts and videos, to
diagnose mental health conditions more efficiently. This study compares the
diagnostic accuracy of mental health identification from social media content and
standard medical examinations. We found that models trained on this data can
accurately predict mental health with around 75% accuracy, similar to the rate
of traditional examinations. Notably, we discovered that specific aspects of
social media content, such as facial expressions and language patterns, are key
indicators of mental health. This study suggests that incorporating social media
data can significantly enhance our understanding of mental health, enabling the
early detection and management of mental health disorders. This technique may
foster a more holistic approach to mental health, allowing healthcare providers to
make more informed decisions based on comprehensive diagnostic results. In the
long term, integrating mental health analysis from social media is set to enable
the early detection and management of mental health disorders, ultimately leading
to a better quality of life for patients. This work has been accepted for oral
presentation at the Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems 2022. 

Keywords: Mental Health, Social Media, Deep Learning, Image and Language Analysis.

A theoretical framework is developed to analyze the impact of costs and constraints on liquid assets on the trading strategies of informed traders. Inhibiting liquid assets' liquidity creates a new source of informed traders' costs, stimulating a complex interaction between multiple types of insiders. In this context, the framework examines the relationship between the costs of liquid assets and the level of liquidity in the market, demonstrating that the market's liquidity is heavily influenced by the costs of liquidating positions. Inhibiting liquidity has a dual effect: reducing the costs of liquidating assets for informed traders who already have positions, but increasing the costs for those who have previously sold their shares. Furthermore, the framework shows that the market's liquidity can be significantly impaired when the costs of liquidating positions exceed a certain threshold, as informed traders engage in a competitive liquidation race. In practice, the model can be applied to various markets by incorporating distinct liquidation costs and constraints, providing a framework for the empirical measurement of liquidity.

Keywords: insider trading, liquidation costs, liquidity constraints, insider herding, liquidation rackets.

The primary goal of intent-based image recommendation is to enhance user experience by providing relevant images in line with their specified intent. Understanding user intent is crucial for producing genuine user experiences and their desired outcomes. However, a major challenge in achieving this is that user intents are not explicitly stated and must be inferred from implicit signals such as search queries and user interactions. To address this, our paper presents a new user intent inference framework that combines the strengths of two existing approaches, a language-based model pre-trained on millions of items, and a neural intent learner that uses unified image features to predict user intents. This paper investigates how principal component analysis handles weighted data in the context of recovering a low-rank matrix from incomplete observations. By considering data as samples from a Gaussian distribution, we demonstrate that principal component analysis is ineffective when applied to weighted combinations of data, whereas techniques that minimize the Frobenius norm of linear combinations are more resilient to noise. These findings are rooted in a stochastic analysis that reveals how PCA's performance is influenced by a statistical measure of low-rank matrices, a concept that is further expanded upon. Ultimately, we relate our results to a recent study by Chen and Petrova (2021) that examined linear combinations in low-rank matrix recovery, largely corroborating their findings. Nonetheless, a notable exception arises when recovering a low-rank matrix from a subset of entries; in this specific case, PCA's weighted counterpart surpasses the baseline method proposed by Chen and Petrova (2021). Ultimately, this investigation highlights the shortcomings of principal component analysis when employed in weighted settings, contributing to a deeper understanding of this widely used dimensionality reduction technique. As such, our analysis may inspire further research on principal component analysis and related topics in matrix theory. The code used to obtain these results is publicly available at https://github.com/berkerman/weighted-PCA. Additionally, this work is supported by NSF grant CCF-1956761. For related work, please see arXiv:2102.10336 and arXiv:2109.04637. Current research is also being extended to incorporate stochastic principal component analysis, a topic of interest in its own right, and preliminary findings can be found at arXiv:2109.04638. Finally, our analysis is being adapted to support the recovery of other structured matrices, such as graphs, at arXiv:2109.04639. This work introduces an EM-based framework, the Semantic Exploit and Maintenance Network, designed to enhance semantic segmentation performance through a multi-scale single-stage detection framework. The framework combines top-performing elements from object detection and semantic segmentation models, incorporating a novel attention mechanism to prioritize semantic information. To refine the model's performance, an EM-based loss function is implemented to minimize errors. The results demonstrate that our framework outperaches existing models in terms of classification and detection precision on the PASCAL VOC 2007 challenge dataset, achieving a 0.5% and 1.2% higher respectively. Furthermore, the framework achieves a mean intersection over union (IoU) of 77.4% and 78.2% on the PASCAL VOC 2012 competition's classification and segmentation metrics, respectively. The framework's remarkable performance is also evident on the ImageNet-Locate competition, achieving a top 1 accuracy of 77.382% and a mean Average Precision (AP) of 87.382% on the validation set. Recent advancements in speech representation learning (SRL) have led to improved performance in speech-related tasks, but they are now facing a growing concern about their vulnerability to malicious attacks. In our research, we assess the robustness of SRL against two types of attacks by two different types of adversaries possessing varying levels of information and resources. By employing a novel white-box attack method that directly manipulates an encoder's parameters, we demonstrate that the model can be compromised with minimal effort by adversaries lacking knowledge of the model. Additionally, our results reveal that the model can also be attacked by an unaware adversary using a transfer attack that utilizes a pre-trained classifier. Our findings further indicate that the representation learned by an autoencoder is more susceptible to malicious alterations than that of a speaker encoder. In conclusion, our study highlights the significant vulnerability of SRL models to malicious attacks and suggests the need for them to be addressed in the future. Furthermore, our research also presents a new challenge for future SRL designs, which could potentially mitigate such threats, and proposes a promising direction for this area by framing the process as a non-cooperative game between the model and adversary. A recently published study examined how API designs in programming languages influence potential security vulnerabilities in cryptographic functions. The research focused on how easy it is for developers to misuse these functions by accidentally calling them with incorrect inputs. A custom tool was developed to measure the susceptibility of each library to misuse, and the study analyzed four cryptographic libraries from three languages: Python, Java, and C. The investigation found that the majority of misuse cases involved incorrect usage of hash functions, which can be mitigated through simple design improvements. Notably, Python's cryptographic libraries were found to have a much higher rate of misuse than those in Java and C. The study's findings are set to be presented at the 2022 Symposium on Security and Usable Programming Languages. 

In this accompanying paper, we detail the creation of our purpose-built tool, Crypter. This tool allows users to create cryptographic libraries by specifying function signatures, function bodies, and test cases. By employing Crypter, we were able to develop a list of potential misuse vectors in the libraries we studied, and our results demonstrate that certain design flaws can significantly increase the likelihood of library misuse. Our research highlights the importance of usable security practices in the development of cryptographic libraries, and the value of our approach lies in its ability to be applied to existing libraries with minimal human intervention. 

Ultimately, our study provides a foundation for future research into the detection and prevention of library misuse, and our results serve as a warning about the potential security risks of certain design choices in cryptographic libraries. The source code for our research is available online, and we hope that our findings will contribute to the ongoing discussion about the design of cryptographic libraries. The ultimate goal of our research is to raise awareness about the potential security risks of library misuse and to drive the development of cryptographic libraries with improved usability. We believe that our research has the potential to make a positive impact on the security of cryptographic libraries, and we hope that our findings will be used to develop libraries that are more robust and secure. 

The key contributions of our research are as follows. (1) The development of a framework for evaluating the susceptibility of cryptographic libraries to misuse; (2) The identification of design flaws that increase the likelihood of library misuse; (3) The presentation of concrete misuse vectors that have been discovered in existing libraries; (4) The demonstration of a more secure design for hash function APIs, and the presentation of test cases that highlight the improved security of this design.

Recent advances in neural network modeling have significantly boosted the performance of part-of-speech tagging.  Unfortunately, traditional models struggle when encountering unknown words in targeted domains, as reliance on pre-trained word embeddings is impractical. This paper introduces a set-valued prediction method to address the challenge. Instead of predicting a single tag for a word, the model predicts a tag set. This not only broadens the prediction scope but also enables a tag set to be the output result. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method yields better outcomes than the baseline comparison. Notably, by incorporating the set-valued prediction, the performance enhancement in unknown word handling is remarkable, with an F1-score increase of 6.2% and 4.3% in the NICT-USApid English and Chinese NER corpora, respectively. Moreover, the method's versatility is further validated through successful applications in zero-shot machine translation and unknown word handling in the context of named entity recognition. The associated source code can be accessed at https://github.com/zhuyibo/set-prediction-pose. A related video presentation is available at https://youtu.be/8t6o6vO6UgA. Ultimately, this work is dedicated to Dr. Zhangjin Huang in commemoration of his birthday. Lastly, the authors would like to acknowledge the valuable guidance provided by Dr. Huang's research in the relevant field. By simulating the qdriven dynamics that occur during the computation, we develop an approach to quantify the accuracy of the approximate VQE output and establish a time frame for when the algorithm reaches its final results under noisy circumstances. This framework enables us to evaluate potential solutions to enhance the performance of the VQE, such as adjusting the variational circuit, changing the loss function, or utilizing a mitigation scheme that counteracts noise effects. Notably, our research finds that applying noise mitigation along with modifying the loss function significantly accelerates the convergence rate of the VQE, achieving a notable speedup under noisy conditions. Additionally, we discover that incorporating a mitigation scheme into the quantum mitigation scheme itself leads to substantial improvements in the algorithm's efficiency, ultimately rendering it more resistant to noise. This work sets the stage for developing more reliable and trustworthy quantum software by providing a thorough understanding of quantum algorithms operating under noisy conditions. In 1999, Hansel discovered an equivariant version of the Brown representability theorem, linking certain functors to equivariant stable homotopy classes. This paper develops Hansel's concept further by introducing Mackey functors as a representation of equivariant homotopy theories within the context of the Goel-Mallick-Sankar model category. These functors demonstrate representability by XrZ-spectra, leading to a generalization of the Goel-Mallick-Sankar construction, enabling the creation of new models for the equivariant stable homotopy category. The work also explores the properties of functors representable by XrZ-spectra, including partial and full triangulated structures, and examines the concept of exponentiation in equivariant stable homotopy theory. These findings reveal that representable spectra exponentiate other functors triangulatedly when the group in question operates freely. A brief examination is also conducted into Mackey functors representable by XZ-spectra, and preliminary results indicate that representable spectra create a full subcategory within the category of equivariant spectra. Further investigation into this subcategory is necessary to confirm whether it comprises spectra with a trivial homotopy layer. The authors also discuss connections between representable spectra and local coefficients, highlighting their significance in topological studies, as well as prospects for future research in equivariant stable homotopy theory. Lastly, the work includes a description of representable spectra as a model for equivariant homology and study groups, demonstrating potential applications in the fields of topology and geometry. These include the computation of equivariant inter sectional homotopy groups and the generalized version of the volume conjecture proposed by Friedhelm Waldorff. The authors plan to explore these topics in detail in future publications. In particular, the last author aims to investigate representable spectra in topological models in forthcoming research, as well as examine the concept of exponentiation in equivariant homotopy theory and its relation to the volume conjecture in [279]. A separate publication is also intended to compute the equivariant inter sectional homotopy groups as part of the work in [280]. A final research paper is expected to create models for the homotopy category of spectra that are equivariantized along the lines of [81] and make connections with the equivariant inter sectional homotopy groups from [280]. In addition to the above, the first author aims to investigate representable spectra in the context of Drinfeld's theory of quantum groups in [141].

The compatibility of machine learning models used in medicine is compromised due to incompatible data representation, hindering direct interoperability of models across institutions. To address this, we developed highdicom, a Python library that converts medical imaging data into a standardized format compatible with Python's NumPy, ONNX, and PyTorch frameworks. With highdicom, medical imaging data can be easily shared between different programming languages, models, and computational platforms, enhancing collaboration between clinicians, researchers, and software developers. Our utility includes a comprehensive testing suite, which demonstrates the conversion of medical imaging data between its original format and highdicom's standardized representation. Additionally, we successfully translated CT scan data converted by highdicom back into its original format, verifying its reversibility. Our study showcases the effectiveness of highdicom in universally translating medical imaging data, facilitating the sharing of models, data, and knowledge across various domains. For reproducibility, the source code for highdicom is available on the public GitHub repository at https://github.com/harshmccaulley/highdicom.
