We've developed a novel image representation method that integrates the benefits of Gabor Filters and Landmark Detection to create Landmark Gabor Filters, or LGFs. This approach involves detecting key locations in an image and applying tailored Gabor Filters to these specific points, resulting in descriptors that are highly distinct and resilient to changes in orientation. Our experiments demonstrate that LGFs outperform existing Gabor-based methods in terms of robustness to various transformations and noise, and also yield more effective image descriptors when combined with aggressive downsampling. Moreover, LGFs offer improved performance in image retrieval tasks, with notable enhancements in datasets like UKBench and Pascal 3D and comparable results on ImageBIRDS and VOC. Importantly, our method's performance surpasses state-of-the-art approaches across multiple scenarios, including object categorization and 3D shape analysis. We also show that LGFs can be effectively used for object detection, with a proposed method achieving a 67.2% mAP when applied to the Pascal VOC dataset. This performance represents a 6% improvement over the state-of-the-art approach, outperforming various well-established methods. Our source code and pre-trained models are available at https://github.com/bernatperra/FGVC8_2019_LGFT. We have also released a new 3D object recognition dataset called the ICBIRD dataset, consisting of 11,000 images of 100 objects, each captured from 21 different viewpoints. The ICBIRD dataset outperforms existing datasets like ImageBIRDS and SUN3D, with notable features including a large number of objects (100), diverse object views (21), and high-resolution images (1024x768). The dataset is available at https://github.com/bernatperra/ICBIRD. Our method's robustness also enables effective 3D object recognition using only 2D information, with a proposed two-stream model achieving a 90.1% accuracy on the ICBIRD dataset, outperforming existing methods by 21, 18, 14 and 9 percentage points respectively. We establish a key relationship, the relative fundamental lemma, by combining the properties of Grassmann-Lie groups with those of p-adic groups. This relative lemma serves as the foundation for deriving the integration map, which expresses orbital integrals of a p-adic group as the combination of local functions. Utilizing the relative lemma, we can develop a map that relates the cohomology of a Grassmann-Lie group to the space of orbital integrals of a p-adic group. This map, although non-trivial, lacks a straightforward characterization, but we do identify an important subset of orbital integrals that can be characterized through the relative lemma. By focusing on this subset, we demonstrate the integrability of smooth transfer factors, which is instrumental in the study of transfer factors for reductive p-adic groups. This work is an extension of the principles outlined in the "relative trace formula" whose development remains an active area of research. Ultimately, the concepts explored here are integral to the process of decomposing the space of automorphic representations of a global product of two groups, each described by a different type, by utilizing the comparison of traces of endoscopics, a concept derived from the relative fundamental lemma. As a result, this work contributes to an enhanced understanding of the fundamental properties of automorphic representations. In the process, this work is notable for being the first to provide a characterization of the space of orbital integrals in the context of p-adic groups, a concept that has been studied by D. Prasad in his work on the local A B B A conjecture. Moreover, this relative lemma has also facilitated a characterization of the Euler-Poincaré series in the cohomology of Grassmann-Lie groups, thereby resolving a long-standing problem initiated by the work of A. Borel in the early 1960s. In a more specific context, this work is notable for being the first to provide a characterization of the orbital integrals corresponding to anisotropic groups, thereby offering insights into the fundamental properties of automorphic representations. In the final analysis, this characterization highlights the significance of the Grassmann-Lie group in facilitating the comparison of orbital integrals, thereby emphasizing its unique role as a bridge that connects the study of group theory with the cohomology of geometric objects. By integrating both mass decays of the top quark and the Higgs boson into the renormalization group framework, we demonstrate a comprehensive approach to remove the impacts of heavier quarks and mass-related parameters one by one, down to the effects of up quarks and gluons. In our research, we demonstrate that for any graph G with at least five vertices and satisfying the degree difference condition Δ(G) - δ(G) ≥ 1, it has a proper edge-coloring using exactly four colors. This finding extends previous work of Máčka and Vukašinović for graphs with a maximum degree of Δ(G) ≥ 4, and also resolves a problem posed by Alikhani et al. involving certain specific graph families. Additionally, we showcase an infinite family of graph families that require four colors, as well as illustrate that three colors may not always be sufficient for these families. Furthermore, we investigate whether four colors are always necessary for graphs with a specific degree difference condition, and currently have no proof or counterproof for this. Lastly, we provide a brief overview of previously known results related to this topic. A novel COVID-19 virus has spread rapidly around the globe, transforming into a global pandemic and overwhelming global healthcare systems. Accurate diagnosis of the virus is crucial, yet healthcare professionals are presented with significant challenges due to the similarities between COVID-19 and other conditions such as bacterial and viral pneumonia. In this study, a deep learning-based computer-aided diagnosis model is proposed to accurately identify COVID-19 using lung CT scan images and clinical data. Recommendation models are increasingly being equipped with explanations to cede control to end-users and shed light on decision-making processes. Although this enhances user understanding, it also introduces vulnerabilities, as users may exploit reliance on post-hoc explanations to create manipulative queries and sway model behavior. We delve into this type of manipulation and investigate how much users can influence recommended items by asking certain questions. Our findings reveal that, in practice, users can significantly alter recommendations simply by asking explanations. This discovery prompts us to assess the impact of post-hoc explanations on recommendation models, as well as the trade-offs between model accuracy, fairness, and user manipulation, using a variety of datasets and recommendation models. Ultimately, our analysis raises crucial questions about the benefits and drawbacks of incorporating post-hoc explanations into recommendation systems. We recommend developing explanations that are both informative and resilient to user exploitation. Furthermore, future research should explore strategies to mitigate the adverse effects of user reliance on explanations and model explainability techniques that are immune to user manipulation. In the context of distribution-free robust learning, we investigate the requirements that must be satisfied by the shape of the learning samples' probability distributions. Specifically, for any concept class that can guarantee robust empirical risk to decrease over time $t$, we demonstrate that there must exist an upper bound on the radius of the query, related to the H\"older norm. This result restricts the possible exponents of robustness in the order of $t$, as opposed to the scenario of symmetric data distributions where any order is feasible. Our findings reveal that the condition of having bounded radius is a necessary and sufficient criterion for robust learning to occur. Furthermore, we provide illustrations of specific distributions that comply with our established condition while featuring non-intuitive properties regarding robustness, namely, the presence of data points near the boundary of the support and the occurrence of extreme values at any desired time. Our research is an initial attempt to analyze distribution-free data and generalizes the findings of previous studies, while addressing the issue of symmetric data distributions. Additionally, we provide insights into the learning process for specific distributions, such as Gaussian and Poisson, and discuss how our results can be extended to scenarios with pre-existing knowledge. Our study ultimately reveals that distribution-free data poses significant challenges for robust learning compared to the symmetric case. Class imbalance problems are widespread in data mining and machine learning, often occurring in real-world applications where a minority class consistently dominates the majorities due to inherent characteristics. As a result, minority class predictions take precedence over majorities in these scenarios. Research has traditionally focused on oversampling methods to address this issue but our work diverges from that by examining the implementation of undersampling classifiers in the context of imbalanced data sets. We've developed three novel classifiers that use undersampling strategies to create more balanced sub-datasets for classification, drawing inspiration from the majorities. These classifiers generate an adaptive sample of data, trained by two distinct neural network classifiers, to balance the dataset. Through a comprehensive evaluation on 64 imbalanced data sets from the KEEL software library, we've demonstrated the efficacy of our approach and contrasted it with the performance of standard oversampling algorithms and a state-of-the-art undersampling method. Moreover, we've made three pre-trained neural network classifiers available for public use, allowing for replication of our results and integration with the classifiers of choice. Our study contributes to the existing literature by providing insights into the performance of pre-trained neural network classifiers on imbalanced data sets, and serves as a foundation for future research on the application of pre-trained models to data imbalance problems. The proposed classifiers are unique in that they differ from traditional oversampling methods by creating minority class predictions without generating new samples, and differ from undersampling methods by directly addressing minority class predictions through the direct manipulation of majority samples. The classification accuracy of the pre-trained neural network classifiers has shown to surpass that of the random undersampling method in many cases, highlighting their potential as a versatile and efficient data preprocessing strategy. Our work suggests that pre-trained models can serve as a valuable starting point for addressing imbalanced data set classification problems, and may also facilitate transfer learning applications in the future. The proposed classifiers are currently implemented in the KEEL software platform and are accessible via the KEEL repository. Our methodology and experimental design are detailed in Section IV, with the results presented in Section V. The conclusions and future research directions are outlined in Section VI. The process of evaluating, comparing, and advancing both automated and human-based document analysis is hindered by a major challenge: identifying relevant datasets. There is an overwhelming abundance of publicly accessible datasets in the field of historical document analysis, making it a laborious task to determine which ones are suitable for novel algorithms and applications. This study aims to provide a comprehensive overview of publicly available handwritten text dataset resources, specifically tailored for historical document analysis, with a focus on those utilizing the Latin script. We have curated a total of 142 datasets in this selection, with a concentration on those employing machine-readable formats and incorporating both training and testing sections. This collection is intended to serve as a valuable resource not only for researchers but also for practitioners, Clusters of datasets are also proposed to address questions such as: which datasets can be utilized for fine-tuning advanced, deep-learning models? Which datasets are suitable for validating model robustness in the context of different writing periods, styles, and formats? Lastly, we outline future avenues of research, with a particular emphasis on developing methods to assess the performance of document and layout analysis in the context of historical document analysis. Using a dataset of hospital episodes in England between 1999 and 2013 that ended in myocardial infarction, we applied techniques from complex network theory to analyze the development and spread of co-occurring health conditions over time. By representing the appearance of new conditions in individual patients as activation patterns, we created a directed network where patient pairs were connected if they had overlapping patterns of conditions at any point within an eight-year window. As patient ages were binned uniformly, the resulting network exhibited the characteristics of a directed complex network, complete with temporal variations in its structure. A critical aspect of our findings lies in identifying socio-demographic influences, such as sex and ethnicity, on the emergence of specific long-term health conditions associated with myocardial infarction, as well as the impact of time since myocardial infarction on the structure of the network. Furthermore, by analyzing the oldest layer of this network, we were able to infer the initial state of the network and set boundaries on the time required for activation patterns to spread throughout the population. Specifically, it took approximately 4-7 years for patterns to reach a significant portion of the population, with or without the influence of individual patients from the oldest layer. Lastly, in exploring the relationship between network structure and patient outcomes following myocardial infarction, we found that patients with a combination of specific long-term conditions had significantly higher mortality rates. In total, our study provides a comprehensive examination of the mechanisms driving the emergence and spread of co-occurring health conditions in the context of myocardial infarction, shedding light on both socio-demographic influences and the structural properties of these networks. Amorphous materials without a crystalline structure are becoming increasingly popular
for their versatility in various applications, from flexible electronics to strong
sports equipment. Research has shown that many amorphous materials behave in a
mechanically similar way to crystalline materials. The study of how different
regimes of plasticity affect a material's mechanical response, particularly at a
microscopic scale, has been limited until now. In this research, we have created a
micro-crack model that simulates the progressive deformation of amorphous materials
subject to increasing stress. The model accounts for the gradual development of new
cracks and the weakening of existing ones, allowing it to simulate the material's
progress towards eventual fracture. The model has been validated by comparing its
output to results from laboratory tests and it has been discovered that both small
and large scale crack growth occur at a similar rate of work hardening, which is
at odds with theoretical predictions of crack acceleration due to loss of cross
section. The study has also highlighted the importance of stress relaxation in the
material due to backflow in the crack tip region, which is shown to be an order of
magnitude slower than bulk relaxation but still plays a significant role in the
mechanical behavior of the material. The model has been further modified to take
into account the gradual separation of particles at crack tips and the resulting
loss of cross-section, which has been found to accelerate crack growth in a way
that is consistent with experimental observations of a near-threshold plateau in
fracture energy. The model has been successfully applied to a range of amorphous
materials, which further validates its accuracy. The study concludes by raising
the possibility that the near-threshold plateau observed in these materials may
be a result of optimal design rather than an inherent property of the material. 
The model, its code and the relevant experimental data can be accessed at 
https://github.com/teodorian/micro_crack_j. The study's findings suggest that 
amorphous materials may be more resistant to fracture than commonly believed. 
The model, though simple in nature, has been found to accurately simulate the 
mechanical response of a variety of different materials, which highlights its 
robustness. The model further emphasizes the importance of considering the 
material's bulk relaxation processes in addition to loss of cross-section when 
predicting fracture, which is a common oversight in theoretical models of 
fracture. Overall, the study provides new insights

Policy cloning, which utilizes supervised learning, is an effective strategy 
for transferring an expert's behavior to a student policy. However, conventional
cloning may not be suitable for complex high-dimensional control issues due 
to the difficulties in creating adequate, dense reward maps. Augmented policy 
cloning addresses this challenge by leveraging the expert's prior knowledge 
embedded within its decision-making process. In this research, we further 
developed augmented policy cloning by incorporating contextual reward information.
The method we created does not necessitate any modifications to the expert, 
instead utilizing contextual data, such as images, to produce a reward function 
for the student. Context-augmented policy cloning demonstrates superior 
performance compared to traditional cloning in a challenging, 95-dimensional 
robot arm control task. The results show that our approach achieves a significant 
reward increase of 15% and outperforms a comparable imitation learning method 
by 40% in terms of success rate. Context-augmented policy cloning was applied 
in a multi-agent setting with promising results, and it has the potential to 
facilitate the transfer of complex robotic skills across various domains. 
Additionally, our study provides new insights into the structure of contextual 
reward maps within expert agents, thereby shedding light on their decision-
making processes. Overall, the work highlights the importance of contextual 
information in transferring knowledge between agents with high degrees of freedom. 
It also showcases the potential of supervised learning to facilitate more 
efficient and semi-supervised imitation learning. The code used in this study 
is publicly accessible at https://github.com/krishanp1/contextual_policy_cloning. 
Further research is required to determine whether augmented policy cloning can 
be applied to diverse imitation learning problems. The code used in this study

A significant number of languages have historical, geographical, or cultural ties, suggesting a strong potential for models in these languages to leverage knowledge from one another. Unfortunately, training multiple models from scratch to transfer knowledge between them is impractical and likely infeasible for most organizations, and even the most advanced training methods may struggle to fully capitalize on this potential. We argue that transfer learning can be more effective when trained models are used to refine other models, and we test this hypothesis across several languages that share a common origin. Our results indicate that this "sequential transfer learning" approach yields better results on various tasks and outperforms traditional fine-tuning, often by a significant margin, in multiple target languages. These improvements are particularly notable in models that have not benefited from previous tasks, and our data suggests that the gain from sequential transfer is linked to the degree of task similarity. We anticipate that our findings will motivate the development of training strategies that facilitate knowledge sharing among related languages, and we envision a future where organizations can more effectively invest resources in developing models for these languages. Ultimately, by leveraging the potential for knowledge transfer and exchange between models, we believe it is possible to achieve significantly better language models than would be feasible through independent training. The code and data used in our research are publicly available at https://github.com/jblew/sequential-transfer-learning. Our models, which achieve state-of-the-art results on various tasks, will be made available through the Hugging Face Transformers library. Additionally, we release the knowledge distillation component of our approach as an open-source framework, which can be utilized for transfer learning between any two pre-trained language models. The assessment of a driver's competence is a critical element of driver training, involving the evaluation of their behavior behind the wheel based on their actions and the surrounding road conditions. Expert drivers, having undergone comprehensive training, serve as a benchmark against which novice drivers are measured. Current methods for driver assessment rely on automated algorithms to collect data, however, these algorithms can miss essential contextual information, thereby creating inconsistencies in driver evaluations. To address this issue, we are exploring a more effective approach that incorporates expert input to measure a driver's competence. Specifically, we are utilizing a supervised learning technique, masked language modeling, to create a more sophisticated estimator that takes into account both the driver's actions and the surrounding road conditions as reported by expert drivers. By doing so, we can capture the nuanced driving behaviors exhibited by experts and novices in various driving situations. As a result, we can integrate expert input to significantly boost the performance of our estimator, achieving comparable accuracy to that of experienced human evaluators. Moreover, our estimator demonstrates adaptability when provided with customized knowledge by an experienced driver, thereby allowing it to assess the driving skills of other experienced drivers, even if they are driving in different geographic locations or during different time periods. Ultimately, our research offers a promising solution for automating driver assessment, potentially reducing the need for human evaluators in the process. Furthermore, our model has the added benefit of being extensible to other areas, such as autonomous vehicles, where it can be utilized to create detailed driving manuals based on the behaviors of experienced drivers. The research findings are set to be released publicly in the near future, at least in part. The code used to train our model is currently available on a public repository at: https://github.com/ylai1988/DriverAssessment. The dataset employed in this study is a modified version of the GDC dataset, a publicly accessible driving record from Geely Technology Group. We have explored using a self-consistent mean-field theory to investigate an implicit-solvent, implicit-surface model of a charged soft plate in an electrolyte solution. This model involves simplifying the solvent to a mean-field potential, effectively merging the solvent and surface degrees of freedom. This allows us to analyze various electrolyte solutions, from diluted salt to polymeric systems, to study how increasing ionic size affects the electrostatic properties near the surface. These calculations are compared with explicit simulations, revealing agreement in key electrostatic characteristics and the influence of ionic size. This implicit-surface model can also be used to study charged microfluidic systems, providing insight into their behavior. The model has been successfully applied to mimic the properties of monovalent salt, polyelectrolyte solutions, and even the coexistence of water and fluorocarbon gases with charged surfaces. Additionally, we have derived a simplified analytical solution, yielding an explicit expression for the surface charge density, which aligns with our implicit-surface model results. Overall, our implicit-surface model provides a valuable tool for designing, simulating, and optimizing charged microfluidic systems, including fluidic diodes, sensors, and interfaces with fluorocarbon gases. This model can be particularly beneficial in designing, simulating, and optimizing microfluidic systems when explicit simulations become computationally infeasible. While our implicit-surface model is primarily suited for charged soft surfaces, it may also be applied to modeling dielectric microfluidic diodes and fluidic diodes made from dielectric materials. Future research could involve extending our implicit-surface model to account for surface charge relaxation, surface friction, and the presence of multivalent ions. Furthermore, we have identified areas for further investigation into the coadsorption of salt and polar molecules, the fluorination of surfaces, and the dielectric properties of diode microstructures. We investigate the performance of hybrid models that combine data and structured knowledge on specific domains in the context of text summarization. Through an experiment involving summarization of scientific research papers, we examine whether models that incorporate incomplete knowledge can rival those solely reliant on data. Our key findings indicate that models merging data and structured knowledge are more efficient in terms of training data required, yet less effective overall when compared to models utilizing only textual inputs. Our research further reveals that the inclusion of domain-specific knowledge, even if partially incorrect, enhances the model's comprehension of scientific terminology, leading to better performance on summarization tasks for scientific research papers. Our model, trained with imperfect knowledge, is more computationally efficient, enabling summarization of input data in 0.03 seconds, significantly outperforming popular text summarization models, such as BART and T5. Our work demonstrates the feasibility of developing text summarization models utilizing partial domain knowledge, contributing to the understanding of hybrid models that integrate data and structured knowledge. Investigations into the behavior of glass-forming liquids often yield contradictory insights. Dynamic properties typically indicate a transition towards a more rigid state, yet this is not supported by equilibrium measurements. One of the primary obstacles in understanding this phenomenon is the absence of an established theoretical framework. Despite this, researchers have been able to analyze dynamic features using a method called thermodynamic scaling. This scaling relations are applied to complex systems in order to simplify their behavior, making it easier to understand. Here, we explore the application of thermodynamic scaling to describe the behavior of a detailed model of the supercooled liquid and glass in silane-methane. We are able to validate that this model replicates the behavior observed in other detailed models of supercooled liquids and glasses, including simulations of fragments and binary mixtures of alkanes. Furthermore, we are able to use this validated model to study the relationship between dynamic and equilibrium properties in greater detail. We are able to simulate liquid-gas phase separation and confirm that freezing occurs when the liquid becomes less dynamic, yet this is not an all-or-nothing process - rather, the process of freezing is characterized by a gradual decrease in dynamic behavior. Freezing is associated with a significant change in dynamic behavior but this change does not mirror the changes observed in equilibrium property diagrams. Freezing is associated with the realization of a more compact state that is less dynamic but this realization is not an end-point. Rather, the process of freezing can be seen as an early stage in a longer-term process of becoming less dynamic. It is possible to slow down this process of becoming less dynamic by increasing temperature. Consequently, thermodynamic scaling provides a framework for understanding how dynamic features relate to equilibrium measurements and how freezing can be seen as an early stage in a longer-term process. This framework is relevant to studies of glass-forming liquids and contributes to the development of a theoretical understanding. It is applicable to simulations of bulk materials and mixtures, suggesting that thermodynamic scaling provides a universal feature. The findings are supported by simulation data and indicate that thermodynamic scaling is relevant to studies of condensed-matter physics. A cotangent bundle of a convex variety exhibits properties beyond those of a symplectic manifold, including unique Hamiltonian flows, which are inherently transverse to the fibers of the projection map. This line of inquiry yields novel curvature weights, which are symplectic analogues of the second fundamental form of a Riemannian manifold, but expressed using cotangent bundle symplectic forms. We introduce LaViSE, a novel text generator specifically designed to create human-like captions for the learned visual features within convolutional neural networks. LaViSE produces captions by optimizing a continuous latent space, which is then used to select an attentioned image region and subsequently generate a description via the Transformer encoder decoder framework. LaViSE has a highly interpretable structure that applies attention globally, thereby enabling the use of pre-trained, language-model-based decoders to produce text descriptions. LaViSE's performance surpasses that of the state-of-the-art in visual captioning, as evident from our experiments using pre-trained CNNs employed in image classification tasks. Additionally, we extend LaViSE to identify the most informative layers within pre-trained networks by modifying the objective function, which results in the discovery of certain remarkable properties. For instance, we found that certain networks employ a pre-trained 'ResNet-101' layer as a common common low-level image descriptor. We believe that LaViSE offers a unique approach to understanding the internal workings of pre-trained networks, which have thus far been regarded as opaque. We propose creating a 1D material with a design inspired by the 1D form of La$_2 -$Sr$_2 $CuO$_4 $, specifically the undoped compound La$_2 $A$_2 $Cu$_3 $O$_7 $ with A = alkaline earth elements. Utilizing our knowledge of the chemical stability of the compounds and the capabilities of solid-state synthesis, we select A elements with similar sizes in the 4d series (Ba, Y, and Cd) to synthesize and study the 1D material. We successfully synthesized single-phase samples of La$_2 $Ba$_2 $Cu$_3 $O$_7 $, with an undoped 1D form similar to that of superconducting La$_2 -$Sr$_2 $CuO$_4 $, and verified its structure through X-ray diffraction, with a hexagonal unit with $P\overline{3} m 1$ space group and a hexagonal chain of Cu-O-Cu. Magnetic property measurements of La$_2 $Ba$_2 $Cu$_3 $O$_7 $ show a paramagnetic behavior consistent with a single magnetic ion, with no superconducting transition observed, and a similar magnetic moment to that of the 2D compound La$_2 -$Sr$_2 $CuO$_4 $, indicating that the unique structure of the 1D compound may not be necessary for high-temperature superconductivity in cuprates. This study also provides a significant contribution to the understanding of high-temperature superconducting cuprates, with implications for the design of superconducting materials at even higher temperatures. Furthermore, the 1D structure of La$_2 $Ba$_2 $Cu$_3 $O$_7 $ may serve as an optimal starting point for developing novel functional materials, such as quantum magnets, with novel magnetic properties and magnetic behaviors. Finally, the success of this study also showcases an innovative method for synthesizing previously unknown compounds, which may provide new opportunities for the synthesis and study of previously unreported compounds.

Our findings indicate that patient familiarity with travel times to facilities and accessibility measures are crucial factors influencing attendance. Meanwhile, demographic factors such as gender and the patient's initial CD4 count play a relatively minor role in determining attendance rates. This knowledge can inform the implementation of interventions at a population level in South African communities. Specifically, initiatives to educate patients about travel times and clinic hours, as well as improving general accessibility, are likely to increase HIV care facility attendance. This highlights the value of considering a range of factors, from travel times to demographic characteristics, in developing predictive models for treatment coverage. We introduce the concept of a proximal mapping on a Banach space, considering it in relation to monotone mappings and the proximal mapping of convex functions. We then establish the existence of a fixed point for the Moreau proximal mapping under certain conditions, also showing that its fixed points coincide with the solutions of an equilibrium problem formulated by Aubin and Frankowska in 1991. Building upon this discovery, we derive key implications, particularly concerning the relationship between Nash equilibrium points and the fixed points of the Moreau proximal mapping when applied to monotone problems whose proximal mapping is upper semicontinuous. One notable outcome of our analysis is the demonstration that the fixed points of the Moreau proximal mapping under our specific conditions can be obtained through the construction of a lower semicontinuous Lagrangian function, whose critical points are also the fixed points of the mapping in question. Our findings are then illustrated by two concrete applications to Nash equilibrium problems and variational inequalities. We also provide an example to illustrate that the fixed points of the Moreau proximal mapping do not necessarily constitute to assure the upper semicontinuity of the mapping's proximal problem. Our research is grounded in the earlier works of Aliprantis et al. (1995), Wu (2007), Agarwal et al. (2010), Aghezaei et al. (2018), and Cian (2019). Comprehensive literature reviews are also provided throughout the paper. The primary contributions of our work reside in its provision of new, general conditions under which the fixed points of the Moreau proximal mapping correspond to the solutions of equilibrium problems as posited by Frankowska (1991) and its derivation of novel, significant implications for the mapping in question. Our work is an extension of the research conducted by Aghezaei et al. (2018), offering a fresh perspective that diverges from the approach employed by Cian (2019). Deep learning models are commonly adopted in the field of process monitoring due to their exceptional predictive capabilities. The predictive distribution can be utilized to quantify the models' limitations, accommodating uncertainties in process data. A Bayesian deep learning framework is applied to a combined convolutional neural network and autoencoder, which are initially trained in an maximum likelihood setting. The uncertainty in the autoencoder's output is subsequently analyzed to predict future process values. Two approaches for assessing uncertainty are presented, which involve simulating multiple samples from the predictive distribution generated by the Bayesian model. These methods are applied to both simulated and actual industrial data sets, which include variables related to steel production. The results demonstrate that employing Bayesian methods can effectively capture the models' limitations without compromising their ability to fit the data. Moreover, the Bayesian approach is found to outperform the traditional maximum likelihood training, especially when the models are subjected to novel, unseen data. Based on these findings, it is recommended that practitioners initially utilize a Bayesian framework when implementing deep learning-based process monitoring systems. Furthermore, it is established that the accuracy of a deep learning model is not inevitably diminished when it is subjected to novel data, given the presence of a strong prior learned by the model. The proposed uncertainty assessment methods can also be extended to other applications beyond process monitoring, such as speech recognition. Future work is likely to involve the application of deep learning-based methods to diverse fields where uncertainty assessment is crucial. Overall, the use of deep learning with uncertainty quantification has the potential to greatly enhance the accuracy and reliability of automated decision-making systems. Convective dynamo models, crucial for understanding solar and stellar magnetic activity, have traditionally been limited to simple models of turbulence that are easy to analyze. However, these simplified models may not accurately represent all the effects that turblent mixing has on magnetic fields. This study explores the impact of these omitted effects on the convective dynamo, specifically looking at how they influence the dynamics of mean-field dynamos. The investigation involves two approaches: examining the individual consequences of these effects and integrating them into a mean-field model. The results show that a combination of these effects can significantly alter the dynamo's behavior, particularly in how helicity is generated and preserved. This has important implications for understanding the dynamics of fast- and slow-convective dynamos, as well as for determining the relevance of Beltrami dynamos. Ultimately, our findings underscore the necessity of considering all the effects that turbulent mixing has on magnetic fields in order to obtain accurate solutions in astrophysical contexts. Moreover, since the studied effects are not exclusive to turbulent convective flows but can also affect other types of flows (e.g., from accretion disks), they are certainly worthy of further exploration. It is discovered that the rate of energy growth is contingent upon the gradient of this probability density function, and its maximum occurs when this probability density function reaches its peak at the wave phase. Consequently, energy transfer is most efficiently directed towards phases that maximize the particle's resident time at the wave peak. Furthermore, when considering an isotropic phase space, this study demonstrates that the distribution of particles is optimized when it is uniform, thereby facilitating the concentration of energy at the wave's crest. Notably, this phenomenon is distinct from the established plasma instability that occurs at the wave's crest in the absence of phase-matching damping forces. In this particular context, the energy transfer is most active when the wave's frequency exceeds its initial value, whereas it is least active when the wave's frequency is below its initial value. Consequently, the wave's spectrum tends to be shifted towards higher frequencies over time. Conversely, when the wave's frequency is below its initial value, the wave's spectrum tends to be shifted towards higher energies. Ultimately, both phenomena converge towards a stationary state in which the energy in the wave's spectrum is evenly distributed across an ever-narrowing band around its resonant frequency. In the limit where the energy in the wave's spectrum is sufficiently low, the distribution of particles can be approximated as being either isotropic or as consisting of two distinct populations, with one being concentrated at the wave's phase and the other being absent altogether. We have developed a Python library called MuMuPy for computational physics purposes. It's designed to calculate transition probabilities involving dimuonium, a compound formed from two muons, within a static electric field. The library includes precise numerical descriptions of the dimuonium potential and its associated wave functions. MuMuPy offers classes that model the potential and related wave functions at specific points. The library also includes functions to compute transition probabilities between energy levels and between muon exchange states and the associated decay rates. This tool is available for download on GitHub under an open-source license that allows for free use and distribution. Its usage is illustrated through two example use cases. Additionally, we include supplementary material detailing the method used for calculating transition probabilities and dimuonium decay rates. A companion paper provides a more in-depth mathematical description of these calculations. The source code for the calculations presented in that paper can be found alongside MuMuPy. Furthermore, we provide the results of our transition probability and decay rate calculations for reference. These calculations involve a vast range of dimuonium states up to n_max = 1000 and ec_max = 1000, which can be found in the supplementary material. The total number of calculated transitions exceeds 3.5 trillion, and the results are available through a public web interface. This web interface allows users to input parameters to calculate the dimuonium transition probability under a static electric field, and users can access the results by entering muon energies, radial excitations, and electric fields. The same web interface can be utilized to calculate dimuonium decay rates by entering muon exchange excitation and the electric field strength. The results of these calculations can be utilized in accelerator searches for dimuonium transitions. The development version of MuMuPy also includes classes for the Higgs boson and baryons, which will be utilized in future calculations. Future plans include extending MuMuPy to compute dimuonium scattering cross-sections, which will be crucial in muon colliders and other related areas. We re-examine the portfolio optimization problem, focusing on an investor's use of absolute and relative wealth in a u-shaped utility function. Absolute wealth influences the risk level due to a loss-gain symmetry, while relative wealth impacts the equity-to-debt ratio due to a symmetry derived from hidden wealth. We create a dynamic portfolio optimization model incorporating these two symmetries and a factor that accounts for hidden wealth, resulting in a more comprehensive solution than previous relative wealth models. We validate our model through numerical simulations and compare its outcomes to those of utility functions representing linear and log u-shapes. The results demonstrate that our model's solution lies between those of log u-shape and relative wealth symmetries. Furthermore, we observe that our model's solution approaches that of the log u-shape as the relative wealth symmetry weakens and that of hidden wealth symmetry as the relative wealth symmetry intensifies. We also compare our model's outcomes to a constant absolute risk tolerance (CARA) model and a relative wealth symmetry (UH) model, finding that our model's solution is generally between the two, except in scenarios where the relative wealth symmetry dominates when hidden wealth is disregarded. Notably, our model's solution diverges from the CARA model's only when the u-shape is open to the left, indicating that the u-shape's closed nature on the left could potentially replicate the CARA model's solution. We conclude that our model provides a more complete and accurate portfolio optimization solution by considering both absolute and relative wealth symmetries. The task of creating accurate, human-annotated examples for supporting machine learning is crucial for numerous natural language processing applications. 

Previous methods, typically employed in settings like semantic parsing, rely on active learning, which selects examples based on uncertainty measures and annotates them, after which the model is retrained and the process repeats until convergence. However, this approach is expensive due to its iterative nature, and a widely used alternative is to employ data scientists to manually annotate a large dataset, followed by pre-training, resulting in benefits such as improved target language quality, enhanced model performance, and more efficient data scientist time. 

We introduce a new qualification pipeline that achieves high-quality results in supporting examples for an automatic summarization task, unlike previous methods which focused on semantic parsing. The pipeline consists of three steps: first, it uses data scientists to generate initial support examples from raw data, then it employs human evaluators to review these examples based on their utility and specifies which ones are considered reliable, and finally it utilizes the selected, high-quality examples to pre-train a model, which is later fine-tuned on labeled data. 

Through our experiments, we compared the performance of models trained with various types of examples, including those actively selected, the initial, low-quality examples, and the high-quality, human-curated examples. The results show that the examples with precise, detailed annotations, provided by data scientists, are the most beneficial for the model, also highlighting the importance of having high-quality examples, even if they are not as numerous. The final, optimized model achieved an 82.6 F1 score, representing a relative improvement of 33.3 compared to the baseline model. The model also outperformed one that utilized active learning, achieving an 8.1 F1 score gap. The new qualification pipeline we introduced can efficiently generate high-quality support examples, leading to improved model performance, making it a valuable approach for various applications. The method we presented is innovative as it addresses a distinct problem, differs from previous methods, and is applicable in real-world scenarios. Recent advancements in pre-trained visual-linguistic models have significantly enhanced text-video retrieval performance. However, existing approaches typically rely on coarse-grained optimization techniques, neglecting to precisely fine-tune the detailed video structure within the learned text-based representations. As a result, the video features propagated from the image backbone to the text encoder lack the necessary spatial-temporal precision required to accurately capture query semantics and align with video contents. To address this limitation, we introduce TS2-Net, a novel model that simultaneously refines the text-based representation and the video structure within the learned model. Specifically, we utilize a novel transformer block to refine the video structure, which is then combined with the propagated video features and propagated through the text encoder. By simultaneously learning the text-based representation and the video structure within the learned model, TS2-Net precisely propagates spatial-temporal video features to accurately capture query semantics and align with video contents. As a result, TS2-Net significantly improves performance over current state-of-the-art approaches across multiple benchmark datasets. For example, it achieves an impressive 12.73% absolute improvement over TM-Adapter on ActivityNet v2 at recall@1. Notably, TS2-Net also outperforms other approaches that focus on refining the text-based representation or the video structure, demonstrating its effectiveness. Our code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/ling-ucla/TS2-Net. We hope that TS2-Net's performance will serve as a new baseline for text-video retrieval benchmarks. Furthermore, the LHCb's research in rare top decays can also be complementary to the searches being conducted by the ATLAS and CMS at the same time, which focuses more on the comprehensive inclusive and semi-inclusive cross-sections of top quarks. Therefore, the sensitivity to the new physics models achieved through the LHCb's analysis of rare top decays is particularly noteworthy, given it is performed outside the main scope of top quark studies by the other two main detectors. In this research, we examine the potential of the LHCb to identify the rare top decays $t\to u\gamma$ and $t\to 3u$ quarks and calculate their production rates and decay widths. We introduce KERES, a novel approach that effectively models diverse kernel ridge regression (KRR) problems through the unsupervised learning of data features. By representing kernel functions as trees, KERES can automatically detect the data's primary characteristics, eliminating the need for user-defined features. This is made possible by leveraging the theoretical connection between KRR and decision trees. Furthermore, our method identifies an approximation of the KRR loss function's Hessian matrix, utilizing the unsupervised features learned and their corresponding generalization errors to achieve robust estimation. This robust estimation enables the model to achieve better generalization by consistently approximating the KRR risk, thereby establishing a reliable supervised learning framework from the unsupervised features derived from the tree representation. In an effort to enhance model interpretability, KERES's ability to derive unsupervised features plays a crucial role. Moreover, the Hessian matrix estimated through the robust unsupervised loss enables the model to provide predictive uncertainty measures, thereby complementing the KRR robustness analysis. Experimental evaluations conducted on various real-world datasets demonstrate the efficacy of KERES, showcasing its ability to produce robust and consistent supervised learning outcomes, while also highlighting its potential applications in feature engineering, adversarial robustness, and predictive uncertainty estimation. KERES's source code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/JoaoPedroZangari/KERES. Additionally, our code used the LightGBM library for tree-based model implementation. We also utilized the Pytorch framework for the actual experiments conducted, making further specifications available in the code repository. During the training of sparse neural networks, there's a delicate balance between exploring possible solutions and exploiting the current one to optimise accuracy.  Conventional methods often suffer from getting stuck in local minima due to an overemphasis on current accuracy.  On the other hand, methods focusing solely on global exploration often delay network pruning until after initial training, which can result in poorly adapted networks.  Our proposed Spartan method aims to improve network sparsity by regularising the relationship between weights and their availability, using a novel approximation of entropy to encourage the network to discover more sparse configurations.  By integrating re-initialisation into the sparsification process, we can assess the network's potential for improved sparsity and accuracy, which is supported by our experimental results showing state-of-the-art performance on image classification tasks at various sparsity levels.  Our code is now publicly available to facilitate further research.  Spartan has achieved superior results on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and ImageNet datasets across multiple sparsity settings, outperforming competing methods by approximately 1.1% on ImageNet when trained to 75% sparsity.  According to our findings, Spartan can achieve up to 7x reduction in parameter space without compromising accuracy compared to their dense counterparts.  Our results also indicate that the network architecture plays a significant role in the sparsity level required to achieve optimal results, which is not commonly addressed in existing research.  Our findings suggest that simpler architectures like ResNet-20 require lower sparsity levels (75%) to achieve similar accuracy, whereas more complex architectures like ResNet-50, require significantly higher sparsity levels (98%) to achieve optimal results. Our results show that the accuracy achieved by Spartan at various sparsity levels is consistently superior to competing methods.  Our results are based on an evaluation of the Spartan method using the Pytorch framework.  Our code is now publicly available at https://github.com/alexgmatheas/sparnan.

Real-world graphs are dynamic in nature, with nodes and edges changing over time, as opposed to static graphs which are often considered in research. Embedding dynamic graphs into continuous spaces poses challenges due to the shifting identities of nodes and the disappearance of temporal relationships. This study investigates various techniques for adapting static graph representation learning to dynamic graphs, with a particular focus on incorporating time aspects. We also introduce a framework for evaluating continuous-time dynamic graph representation learning, which includes methods utilizing continuous-time matrix factorization, temporal point process networks, and temporal network embedding. Our experimental findings reveal that the performance of these methods can depend significantly on the choice of loss function and optimization procedure. Therefore, we propose a general loss function and a larger and more comprehensive dataset of graph, with DynBG-1000, consisting of 100 time-stamped interactions among 1000 nodes. Our results also show that DynBG-1000 supports the development and testing of dynamic graph representation learning methods over extended periods of time. Moreover, we observe that the method of temporal network embedding, although originally designed for static graphs, can be effective in learning dynamic graph representations, with DynBG-1000, with a surprising finding that adding more time-stamped interactions can actually lead to lower accuracy. Our study provides a foundation for future research in dynamic graph representation learning. The code and DynBG-1000 are publicly available at https://github.com/quantopedia/Dynamic-Graph-Representation-Learning. A constraint-abiding agent is designed to learn constraints implicitly while focusing on its primary goal. This concept is crucial, as individuals and organizations frequently have underlying constraints that cannot be compromised. While researchers have extensively investigated agents that optimize multiple objectives, the idea of integrating constraints that are not directly tied to rewards is still evolving. Our work explores the theoretical benefits of learned constraints in the context of reinforcement learning, applying three types of constraints - prescriptive, descriptive, and objective constraints - to three scenarios. This classification helps clarify the distinction between constraints that define what actions can be taken and those that provide underlying reasons for inaction. Moreover, this taxonomy highlights the difference between constraints that directly influence reward functions and those that do not. To illustrate the utility of this framework, we illustrate the combination of these constraint types with Q-learning agents, demonstrating both positive and negative outcomes. These results emphasize the importance of incorporating constraints explicitly, especially when agents fail to generalize constraints to zero-valued Q-values. Additionally, we show that descriptive constraints can be leveraged to improve exploration but only if the constraints accurately represent the environment. Finally, we suggest the concept of objective constraints, enabling the integration of domain-specific security constraints with general reward functions, thus facilitating the design of secure reinforcement learning agents. These findings indicate that the learned constraints of a constraint-abiding agent can be beneficial in the context of reinforcement learning but also present significant challenges to their effective integration. Ultimately, we believe that the distinction between constraints that directly impact reward functions and those that do not provides valuable insights for future research in this domain. Our work provides a theoretical foundation for future investigations into the integration of constraints in reinforcement learning settings. While our analysis is theoretically based, we acknowledge that the practical implementation of constraint integration is also an important area of study. As such, we encourage researchers to further explore both the theoretical and practical implications of our results. Ultimately, we hope that our work contributes to a deeper understanding of the complex interplay between constraints, goals, and learned behavior in the context of reinforcement learning. In the remainder of this document, we elaborate on the concept of prescriptive, descriptive, and objective constraints, provide examples of each, and explore their potential integration with Q-learning agents. Furthermore, as a practical illustration of our findings, we present a reinforcement learning agent designed to gather information about a dynamic environment while avoiding certain actions that are detrimental to its health. This agent serves as a constraint-abiding agent, as it learns three constraints - the presence of pits, the presence of enemies, and the presence of health sources -

Machine learning and physics have become increasingly intertwined in "physics-informed neural networks" (PINNs). We developed an iterative method for calculating the accuracy of PINNs that utilizes the resolution of a non-linear integral equation. This technique combines numerical methods for evaluating the accuracy of PINNs with a posteriori error estimation methods. As a result, we can certify predictions made by PINNs within a specified scope. Our approach is demonstrated by the solution of two test problems. These examples show that even with approximate numerical solutions and approximations of the stability factor, our method yields reliable error estimates. We also compared its performance with a more sophisticated method that uses a more precise estimate of the stability factor, revealing that our approach is generally more effective. This new method has the advantage of being easier to use and less computationally demanding. These findings open up the possibility of applying our method to a wide range of applications, including complex ones. One such example is the numerical simulation of a Bratu-type problem in a two-dimensional domain. Here, we used a variational network to approximate the solution and combined it with our iterative method for calculating the accuracy of PINNs. The results show that our method allows us to certify the results accurately despite some imprecision in the variational network, which in this case amounts to a relative error of 0.0174. These findings highlight the value of our method in confirming the accuracy of variational approximations and PINNs in particular. They also show that these approximations can be reliable, even if they are not exact. Furthermore, we verified that our method confirms the findings from a more recent study, which used a more sophisticated method to calculate the accuracy of PINNs. These findings demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in facilitating the use of variational approximations and PINNs to solve a wide range of physical problems. They also show that these approximations can be reliable, even if they are not exact. They also reveal that our method is more effective when the approximate solution is more accurate. These findings are illustrated by the solution of a test problem using a variational network with a relative error of $10^{-4}$. In response, researchers have employed optimization techniques, both directly and through Reinforcement Learning methods, to develop resilience against these threats. However, optimizing robustly is often computationally costly, necessitating a balance between being adversarial-resistant and efficient. Various approaches have been taken to address this challenge, including training models to be robust to potential attacks, learning them incrementally to minimize costs, and utilizing existing knowledge to adapt to new situations quickly. Despite the significant interest in adversarial robustness, few studies have focused on the underlying principles and their interconnections, making it difficult to navigate the existing literature. This survey aims to bridge this gap by exploring the common goals, techniques, and future directions in the field, with a particular emphasis on the adversarial robustness paradigm. We highlight the key distinctions between using Reinforcement Learning to learn strategies and direct gradient optimization, as well as the primary research trends and evaluations. Moreover, we discuss existing evaluations and propose a new framework for assessing the effectiveness of models in the context of adversarial attacks. This framework, grounded in the Defenses-Agents-Attacks structure, can facilitate systematic comparisons between models and facilitate future research. Ultimately, this survey provides a comprehensive overview of the complex and rapidly evolving field of adversarial robustness, with specific regard to Reinforcement Learning. By identifying areas for further research and examining the various approaches, we aim to contribute to the development of robust machine learning models. We propose the Defenses-Agents-Attacks framework as a tool for evaluating the effectiveness of models in the presence of adversarial attacks and facilitate future research. Unlike other solutions, OntoPlot allows for seamless sharing of visualizations through unique, web-accessible URLs, where users can dynamically explore related concepts by clicking on terms, revealing their hidden connections and meanings. Additionally, Style-GAN outperforms existing generative models by generating images at a higher resolution of $256\times256$ pixels, demonstrating its potential in generating realistic, human-like images for applications in computer graphics and machine learning. The accompanying code and models can be found on the dedicated GitHub page. Our research aims to contribute to the advancement of deep learning for generative image modeling and functionality by investigating how latent representations can be controlled and the data distribution can be learned and manipulated. We anticipate that Style-GAN will serve as a foundation for the development of future generative models capable of high-resolution image generation across various domains. We present our findings at the Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR) 2019. We are proud to announce that our research received the Best Paper Award at CVPR 2019, showcasing the innovative capabilities of Style-GAN. The associated video can be found at https://youtu.be/0e8eVx-UIA0. We are committed to providing our research through an open review at arXiv arXiv:1802.105114, encouraging readers to provide their feedback and engage in a constructive discussion to further enhance the development of our research. The open discussion facilitated by the arXiv platform played a crucial role in the refinement of our research, for which we are grateful to the editors and reviewers for their valuable input and guidance. Ultimately, we hope that our research at the intersection of deep generative models and controlled image generation will inspire future innovations and contribute to the advancement of the field. Our analysis is centered on the behavior of binary mixtures consisting of spherical molecules, with a particular emphasis on systems where one molecule has two freely rotating parts. We develop a mathematical model to determine the thermal diffusion factor under conditions of zero convection using the Chapman-Enskog expansion. This expansion yields a comprehensive expression for the thermal diffusion factor, with terms that are linear, quadratic, and cubic in symmetry, with two rotating degrees of freedom being assumed to be variable. We calculate the individual components of the thermal diffusion factor and find that molecular flexibility has a noticeable impact, particularly at lower temperatures, with non-zero values emerging even in purely thermal scenarios. Furthermore, our results indicate a complex relationship between temperature and molecular polarity, with temperature dependencies that may seem counterintuitive at first glance. We also explore the effects of molecular shape and the variable nature of one system's rotational degrees of freedom on the thermal diffusion factor, with variable freedom resulting in unique and potentially large contributions to the thermal diffusion factor. In general, our findings suggest that molecular flexibility plays a pivotal role in non-uniform thermal processes, with key factors being influenced not only by molecular polarity, shape, but also by rotational states and temperature conditions. We anticipate that our study will provide valuable insights into non-uniform thermal effects, particularly in complex systems where thermal diffusion is influenced by factors beyond conventional non-uniform thermodynamic principles. Recent research suggests that pre-trained language models, especially those based on the Transformer architecture, can achieve state-of-the-art performance in a variety of tasks after fine-tuning. However, the focus has largely been on developing ever-larger models, which may not be justified by corresponding improvements in performance or computational efficiency. This paper presents a different approach by exploring the performance of fine-tuned models for essay scoring tasks, using both smaller and larger models, including those with significantly fewer parameters than the largest models. The study examines the effectiveness of five pre-trained models, including GPT2 and BERT, in conjunction with three simple architectures for the task, and evaluates their performance against a complex multi-task model. The results reveal that smaller models, developed with a more modest number of parameters, can achieve comparable or superior performance to larger models, including those from the BERT-Architecture family. The study also demonstrates that a straightforward combination of performance scores does not accurately reflect the quality of written work, necessitating a more sophisticated evaluation metric. The performance results, code, and model parameters, are available for review on the online platform GitHub at the address https://github.com/alexey-clark/transformer-based-essay-scoring. A companion document provides additional information on the task, models, and experimental results, including descriptions of the pre-trained models, the dataset, the evaluation metrics, and issues encountered during the study. The document can be accessed through the following address: https://github.com/alexey-clark/transformer-based-essay-scoring/raw/master/appendix.pdf. The issue of suppressing false positives in a neural machine translation model contains inherent challenges that make it difficult to tackle through traditional machine learning methods. However, this challenge can be re-framed in a more manageable way by drawing on insights from recent research in unsupervised learning and data re-ranking techniques for ranking problems. Building on this realization, our approach, called FPTP, is developed with the purpose of reducing false positives generated by an NMT model during translation. This approach is designed to be integrated with any existing translation model, making it easy to apply as it relies solely on parallel data, eliminating the need for annotated data for post-editing simulation. Furthermore, our approach enhances the ability of the NMT model to produce high-quality translations with minimal false positives. Comprehensive experiments are conducted to validate the effectiveness of our approach, with results showing that it outperforms existing solutions to the false positive suppression problem, including a recently proposed method. Our findings indicate that FPTP's performance is on par with models that have been trained on annotated data for post-editing simulation. A thorough error analysis is also carried out to gain a deeper understanding of the role of false positives in translation performance. Our research further demonstrates the ability of FPTP to yield high-quality translations with minimal false positives. This capability makes it easier to integrate our approach with other ranking-based metrics to facilitate a trade-off between translation quality and the suppression of false positives. Ultimately, our approach facilitates a more efficient interaction between human translators and machine translation systems, making it easier to rely on machines for translation tasks that were previously manual. This allows for a more natural translation workflow where human editors intervene only when necessary, focusing on improving the translation quality, not the speed, of an NMT model. Our approach is expected to have a significant impact in real-world translation environments, particularly in domains where high-quality translations are critical and the suppression of false positives is essential. A case in point is the recent COVID-19 pandemic, where accurate translation of medical terminology is crucial and a good post-editing simulation is non-negotiable. Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have driven significant progress in the restoration of degraded music. The application of deep learning techniques to enhance the quality of low-quality music recordings is a rapidly developing research area. A crucial challenge in this field involves the effective use of training data, which is often limited. Either due to data scarcity or the labor-intensive process involved, datasets are often restricted to a limited frequency range, such as mono or a specific subset of stereo channels. To address this issue, a novel deep learning model called the Spectrogram Synthesis Network (SSN) is proposed in this paper. SSN generates detailed spectrograms from unutilized data sources, effectively supplementing a training pool with high-quality signals in both mono and stereo channels. The SSN model is versatile, allowing it to work in both single-channel and multi-channel environments. The performance of SSN is compared with existing music enhancement techniques, such as musDBP2P and the Unmixed Spectrogram Synthesis Network. The results indicate that SSN achieves superior results in both subjective and objective performance metrics. Creating realistic motion patterns in animation is crucial for creating believable movements. In this research, we have gathered data on the movements made while throwing objects of different sizes using upper and lower body parts. We have collected this information from actual demonstrations and simulated it using a character animation setup in the hopes of improving animated throwing motions. Our findings suggest that the size and method of throwing are significant factors influencing the overall motion pattern. Despite the challenges of accurately replicating hand and object interactions in throwing motions, our data shows potential for enhancing animated simulations. We have successfully demonstrated how incorporating real motion data can improve the quality of throwing motions in animation. This knowledge can aid artists in creating more realistic movements in future animations. The research data and animation results are available online at the specified URL.

To improve the efficiency of neural machine translation, a new method has been introduced that synthesizes syntax from pre-trained models and combines it with source text features. The proposed method, called SeqSyNMT, enhances the ability of a neural machine translation system to grasp sentence structure and only makes adjustments when necessary, doing so by integrating synthesized syntax with existing source features. The results demonstrate that SeqSyNMT improves translation fluency and reversals (e.g., first translation) without increasing computation. Analysis shows that the inclusion of a syntax-aware attention model significantly impacts translation quality, particularly in sentences with long distances in structure. Furthermore, experiments indicate that SeqSyNMT's benefits are most pronounced in tasks requiring precise translation and in cases where full parsing is not feasible or effective. Ultimately, SeqSyNMT's benefits are seen in three key areas: better translation quality, more natural phrasing, and overall system efficiency. The code for SeqSyNMT is available online. We developed an algorithm for updating the parameters of a statistical model by comparing its predicted output to actual data. Starting with the Bayes Waveform Classifier, we collected GDS event data from two LHC runs with high luminosities, 2.5 and 2.1 times 10^33 cm^2/s, and converted it into event space. We then applied various parameter sets to generate simulated events and compared them to the actual events through a layer of detector simulation. Focusing on four key variables, we calculated the differences between simulated and actual distributions using two metrics, then weighted each parameter set by its similarity and selected the most likely ones based on their combined weights. The resulting parameter sets are generally in line with the Standard Model of particle physics, with some slight deviations that could be the result of minor statistical errors or potential issues with the detector simulation, as the actual LHC data is not yet available for comparison. Furthermore, we successfully applied this algorithm to two different search areas, LHCb's Lambda_bbar overline to K-p pi+ and the Bayes reconstruction of B_s overline to D_s pi+, with the parameter sets obtained mirroring the actual distributions, thereby validating the Bayes Waveform Classifier. Additionally, we demonstrated that the Bayes Waveform Classifier is capable of handling high-speed data with minimal loss of detail, making it a suitable tool for real-time particle identification during data collection. Overall, the proposed algorithm is versatile and can be used in various scientific research applications. Furthermore, its ability to function in real-time, update based on data, incorporate multiple variables, and identify correlations is valuable in machine learning more broadly. Interestingly, the simulations suggest that, assuming the same level of precision as in the current data, the parameter sets obtained would allow for detection of five or six times more events in search area one and two or three times more events in search area two, under the specified conditions. We explore the problem of quantum state learning, focusing on the challenge of reconstructing an unknown quantum state $\rho$ solely based on measurements of an observable $\hat{A$. Two primary approaches exist: one can either estimate the expectation value of $\hat{A$ given the density matrix $\rho$ and then compute $\rho$, or vice versa and estimate $\hat{A$ directly. We examine the most effective strategy and derive a fundamental trade-off influencing performance in this setting: the relationship between the uncertainty of estimating $\rho$ and the expectation value of $\hat{A\rho$. This trade-off holds for any pair of quantum states and an arbitrary observable. We also obtain specific conditions under which direct estimation of $\hat{A$ is preferable to first estimating $\rho$ and computing $\hat{A\rho$. Our results are illustrated with a specific example based on qubit systems. We further discuss how our findings can lead to enhanced quantum state learning protocols. In particular, we outline a method to obtain the Wigner tomographic representation of a qubit's density operator with minimal uncertainty in estimating certain values, ultimately aiming to improve the overall state reconstruction fidelity. The analysis delves into the effects of random sampling on these estimates, examining both the asymptotic behavior and the efficiency in achieving a desired level of precision for the Wigner tomography, as well as the optimal sampling requirements in order to achieve a state reconstruction scheme with the highest possible fidelity. The best known estimate for the variance of the phase of qubit states, which could provide enhanced sensitivity in experiments measuring the phase, is also presented. The approach to achieve this estimate involves using collections of qubit states and their corresponding Wigner images, which provide a set of parameters that can be used to reconstruct any density operator for a qubit. We explore the conditions under which the Wigner image is unique for different states in the sense that it does not exhibit degeneracies, which would complicate state reconstruction. The possibility of using pure states, which have full Wigner images, is of course advantageous in this context. However, we identify a set of mixed states that, despite having the same expectation values for all Wigner images, still allow for unique state reconstruction.
